papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that digit bias in pretraining data (following Benford's Law) is internalized by LLMs, primarily in later-layer FFN neurons, and causally contributes to numerical hallucinations; pruning these biased neurons can mitigate the bias.
papers.conclusion: Digit bias originating from pretraining corpus statistics is a fundamental cause of numerical hallucinations in LLMs, and targeted intervention on biased neurons offers a potential mitigation strategy.
papers.key_findings:
The digit distribution in the pretraining corpus (Olmo-mix-1124) strongly aligns with Benford's Law, favoring smaller leading digits.
LLMs consistently overgenerate smaller digits in numerical reasoning tasks, even when ground-truth digits are uniformly distributed.
The digit bias is primarily driven by a subset of highly digit-selective feed-forward network (FFN) neurons concentrated in the deeper layers of the model.
When the model generates an incorrect answer, the first erroneous digit shows an even stronger skew toward smaller values, following Benford's Law.
Pruning neurons most selective for digit '1' can partially correct erroneous outputs, providing causal evidence that digit bias contributes to numerical hallucination.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are conducted on relatively small-scale decoder-only LLMs (7B–9B parameters); whether similar patterns persist in larger models or Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models remains an open question.
The neuron pruning strategy is coarse and may disrupt correct generations, limiting overall accuracy gains.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to larger models and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures.
Developing more fine-grained or adaptive debiasing methods beyond simple pruning.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit impressive performance on complex reasoning tasks, yet they frequently fail on basic numerical problems, producing incorrect outputs. Inspired by Benford's Law, a statistical pattern in which lower digits occur more frequently as leading digits, we hypothesize that the skewed digit distributions in web-collected corpora may be learned by LLMs during pretraining, leading to biased numerical generation. To investigate the hypothesis, we first examine whether digits frequencies in pretraining corpus (OLMo2) follows Benford's law. We then construct an evaluation benchmark in which the ground-truth digits are uniformly distributed within each of the seven numerical reasoning tasks. Our evaluation results demonstrate that leading open-source LLMs show a consistent pattern of digit bias that resembles Benford's law. Through logit-lens tracing and neuron-level dissection, we identify that this bias arises predominantly from a small subset of highly digit-selective feed-forward network (FFN) neurons in the deeper layers. Finally, we demonstrate that pruning these neurons mitigates imbalanced overgeneration and partially corrects erroneous outputs, providing causal evidence that fine-grained pretraining digit bias can propagate into model behavior. Our findings reveal a fundamental connection between corpus-level statistics and symbolic failure modes in LLMs, offering a new lens for diagnosing and mitigating hallucinations in numerical tasks.

papers.title: On the Interplay Between Fine-tuning and Sentence-level Probing for Linguistic Knowledge in Pre-trained Transformers
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning affect the representations and linguistic knowledge in pre-trained transformer models, and to what extent can changes in probing accuracy be attributed to changes in linguistic knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that fine-tuning pre-trained transformer models affects sentence-level probing accuracy, but these changes are not straightforward and often not due to acquisition or loss of linguistic knowledge; instead, they can be attributed to changes in attention distribution or other factors, requiring careful interpretation.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that fine-tuning can lead to substantial changes in probing accuracy, but these changes require careful interpretation as they may not directly indicate changes in linguistic knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning affects probing accuracy, with changes typically larger for higher layers.
Changes in probing accuracy vary across models, fine-tuning tasks, and probing tasks.
Improvements in probing accuracy with CLS-pooling can be attributed to changes in attention distribution rather than acquisition of new linguistic knowledge.
Fine-tuning can negatively affect probing accuracy, possibly due to changes in representations.
Only in few cases does fine-tuning improve probing accuracy beyond using a strong pooling method like mean-pooling.
papers.limitation: It remains unclear whether fine-tuning indeed removes the linguistic knowledge or whether it is simply no longer linearly separable.
future_direction: Further investigation into whether fine-tuning removes linguistic knowledge or just makes it not linearly separable.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained contextualized embedding models has become an integral part of the NLP pipeline. At the same time, probing has emerged as a way to investigate the linguistic knowledge captured by pre-trained models. Very little is, however, understood about how fine-tuning affects the representations of pre-trained models and thereby the linguistic knowledge they encode. This paper contributes towards closing this gap. We study three different pre-trained models: BERT, RoBERTa, and ALBERT, and investigate through sentence-level probing how finetuning affects their representations. We find that for some probing tasks fine-tuning leads to substantial changes in accuracy, possibly suggesting that fine-tuning introduces or even removes linguistic knowledge from a pre-trained model. These changes, however, vary greatly across different models, fine-tuning and probing tasks. Our analysis reveals that while finetuning indeed changes the representations of a pre-trained model and these changes are typically larger for higher layers, only in very few cases, fine-tuning has a positive effect on probing accuracy that is larger than just using the pre-trained model with a strong pooling method. Based on our findings, we argue that both positive and negative effects of finetuning on probing require a careful interpretation.

papers.title: A Sentence is Worth a Thousand Pictures: Can Large Language Models Understand Hum4n L4ngu4ge and the W0rld behind W0rds?
papers.research_question: Are humans and LLMs equally accurate in decoding leetspeak, and can they equally explain the substitutions?
papers.core_contribution: Humans outperform LLMs in decoding leetspeak, demonstrating that LLMs lack top-down processing and grounded cognition, which are essential for human-like language understanding.
papers.conclusion: LLMs do not possess human-like linguistic competence; superficial similarity in output does not imply system equivalence, and models lack grounded cognition and top-down processing.
papers.key_findings:
Humans achieve near-ceiling accuracy in decoding leetspeak, while LLMs perform worse.
ChatGPT-4o is the best-performing model but still below humans, especially with more substitutions.
LLMs show an accuracy-reasoning mismatch, often decoding correctly but failing to explain substitutions.
Model errors are qualitatively different from human errors, indicating a lack of common sense and real-world grounding.
Performance differences suggest LLMs rely on form-based associations rather than meaning.
future_direction: Future language models may need to take an entirely different approach, beginning with deeper semantics and cognitive models of the world.
A closer examination of how LLM outputs align with subtle syntactic, acceptability judgments in humans.
Combining deep learning with models of symbolic cognition.
papers.abstract: Modern Artificial Intelligence applications show great potential for language-related tasks that rely on next-word prediction. The current generation of Large Language Models (LLMs) have been linked to claims about human-like linguistic performance and their applications are hailed both as a step towards artificial general intelligence and as a major advance in understanding the cognitive, and even neural basis of human language. To assess these claims, first we analyze the contribution of LLMs as theoretically informative representations of a target cognitive system vs. atheoretical mechanistic tools. Second, we evaluate the models' ability to see the bigger picture, through top-down feedback from higher levels of processing, which requires grounding in previous expectations and past world experience. We hypothesize that since models lack grounded cognition, they cannot take advantage of these features and instead solely rely on fixed associations between represented words and word vectors. To assess this, we designed and ran a novel 'leet task' (l33t t4sk), which requires decoding sentences in which letters are systematically replaced by numbers. The results suggest that humans excel in this task whereas models struggle, confirming our hypothesis. We interpret the results by identifying the key abilities that are still missing from the current state of development of these models, which require solutions that go beyond increased system scaling.

papers.title: Predicting Fine-Tuning Performance with Probing
papers.research_question: Can probing results be used to predict the fine-tuning performance of deep NLP models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that probing results can predict fine-tuning performance with errors 40%-80% smaller than baselines, using as few as three probing configurations.
papers.conclusion: Probing can be used to predict fine-tuning performance and has potential to improve model development efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Probing results from as few as three configurations can predict fine-tuning performance with high accuracy.
The most informative probing tasks and layers vary across fine-tuning tasks.
Probing is computationally efficient compared to fine-tuning.
The choice of probing method (e.g., MLP-20, RandomForest-100) affects predictability.
Probing with 400 samples per class still provides predictability, though less than with 1200 samples.
papers.limitation:
The evaluation is limited to classification tasks and may not generalize to other tasks like translation.
The method requires selecting probing tasks and layers, which may not be straightforward.
future_direction: Extending the method to non-classification tasks such as translation.
Incorporating probing into model development pipelines.
papers.abstract: Large NLP models have recently shown impressive performance in language understanding tasks, typically evaluated by their fine-tuned performance. Alternatively, probing has received increasing attention as being a lightweight method for interpreting the intrinsic mechanisms of large NLP models. In probing, post-hoc classifiers are trained on “out-of-domain” datasets that diagnose specific abilities. While probing the language models has led to insightful findings, they appear disjointed from the development of models. This paper explores the utility of probing deep NLP models to extract a proxy signal widely used in model development – the fine-tuning performance. We find that it is possible to use the accuracies of only three probing tests to predict the fine-tuning performance with errors 40% - 80% smaller than baselines. We further discuss possible avenues where probing can empower the development of deep NLP models.

papers.title: StreetMath: Study of LLMs' Approximation Behaviors
papers.abstract: There is a substantial body of literature examining the mathematical reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), particularly their performance on precise arithmetic operations in autoregressive architectures. However, their ability to perform approximate reasoning in informal, fast-paced mathematical operations has received far less attention, especially among non-autoregressive decoder models. Our work addresses this gap by introducing StreetMath, a benchmark designed to evaluate models' approximation abilities under real-world approximation scenarios. We conduct extensive evaluations across different LLM architectures: Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507, Dream-v0-Instruct-7B, Falcon-Mamba-7B-Instruct, and Mamba-GPT-3B. Furthermore, we apply mechanistic interpretability techniques to probe their internal computational states. Our analysis reveals that LLMs generally attempt to compute exact values or invoke external tools even in tasks that call for approximation. Moreover, while models sometimes reach the correct answer in early layers or steps, they still consume more tokens when solving approximation tasks. Additional experiments indicate that exact and approximate arithmetic operations rely on largely separate neural components. Drawing upon research on cognitive psychology, we argue that LLMs do not exhibit cognitive miserliness in the same way humans do in street math settings. We open source our work https://github.com/ctseng777/StreetMath

papers.title: From Next-Token to Mathematics: The Learning Dynamics of Mathematical Reasoning in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does mathematical reasoning ability develop during pre-training and post-training in LLMs, and how aligned are the learning trajectories with human curricula?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MathCAMPS, a fine-grained dataset for mathematical reasoning, and uses it to analyze learning dynamics, showing that mathematical skills are learned in an order correlated with human curriculum and that instruction tuning has varied effects on different skills.
papers.conclusion: MathCAMPS enables fine-grained analysis of mathematical reasoning, revealing insights into learning dynamics and the effects of instruction tuning, paving the way for an empirical understanding of LLM training dynamics in relation to reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Mathematical skills are learned during pre-training in an order that measurably correlates with the human-designed curriculum, even though training data are randomly ordered.
Skills evolve smoothly during training rather than emerging discretely at specific points.
Instruction tuning has varied effects: it improves some mathematical skills but degrades others, and the impact depends on the specific tuning methodology.
Models struggle more with fraction operations than with decimal operations, likely due to tokenization differences and the multi-step reasoning required for fractions.
Models are not robust to follow-up questions, showing significant accuracy drops when probed with incremental or counterfactual questions.
papers.limitation: The evaluation only covers computational problems and does not capture conceptual mathematical skills that human students also learn.
future_direction: Using MathCAMPS to inform model pre-training and evaluation for educational applications.
Using follow-up problems in MathCAMPS as a rich source for further analysis of model robustness and dialogue understanding.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) solely trained on next-token prediction learn to solve a wide range of problems involving mathematical reasoning. But how does this ability evolve during training? We show the first analysis of how mathematical reasoning abilities of several open-weight LLMs develop during pre-training and post-training. To this end, we construct MathCAMPS, a synthetic dataset of novel mathematical reasoning problems grounded in 44 fine-grained skills taken from the Common Core curriculum from K to 8th grades. In one experiment, we show that mathematical skills are learned during pre-training in an order that measurably correlates with the human-designed curriculum, even though training data are randomly ordered. We also show a detailed analysis of which mathematical abilities benefit from instruction tuning, a widely used post-training method and, in contrast, which skills suffer. Our work paves the way for an empirical understanding of LLM training dynamics in relation to reasoning.

papers.title: Understanding the Countably Infinite: Neural Network Models of the Successor Function and its Acquisition
papers.research_question: How do children learn the successor function, what latent number representations make this possible, and what does it mean to understand the countably infinite?
papers.core_contribution: The place-value model shows a drop in representational similarity across tens boundaries, revealing that counting across a tens boundary can be understood as a vector operation in 2D space, and curriculum learning shows sharpening of smaller number representations during development.
papers.conclusion: This study is a first step in using neural networks to understand the successor function, and future work should explore recurrent architectures for modeling the counting process more generally.
papers.key_findings:
The count list model achieved perfect training accuracy but 0% test accuracy, indicating no generalization.
The place-value model showed 24% test accuracy and sensitivity to tens boundaries in representational similarity.
MDS analysis revealed systematic mapping of numbers to successors across tens boundaries in the place-value model.
Curriculum learning simulations showed incremental learning and sharpening of representations for smaller numbers.
The models did not learn the successor function well for the highest test range (81-99) in curriculum learning.
papers.limitation:
The count list model lacks sensitivity to tens boundaries, which is critical for place-value structure.
The place-value model has low test accuracy (24%) and does not generalize perfectly.
The models learn formally different ML tasks, making direct comparison difficult.
In curriculum learning, the highest test range (81-99) was not learned well even with additional training.
future_direction: Move beyond generating the successor of a number to modeling the counting process more generally.
Explore training recurrent neural network models to sequentially count, first to 100 and then arbitrarily high.
Use richer recurrent architectures to learn the recursive structure of natural numbers.
papers.abstract: As children enter elementary school, their understanding of the ordinal structure of numbers transitions from a memorized count list of the first 50-100 numbers to knowing the successor function and understanding the countably infinite. We investigate this developmental change in two neural network models that learn the successor function on the pairs (N, N+1) for N in (0, 98). The first uses a one-hot encoding of the input and output values and corresponds to children memorizing a count list, while the second model uses a place-value encoding and corresponds to children learning the language rules for naming numbers. The place-value model showed a predicted drop in representational similarity across tens boundaries. Counting across a tens boundary can be understood as a vector operation in 2D space, where the numbers with the same tens place are organized in a linearly separable manner, whereas those with the same ones place are grouped together. A curriculum learning simulation shows that, in the expanding numerical environment of the developing child, representations of smaller numbers continue to be sharpened even as larger numbers begin to be learned. These models set the stage for future work using recurrent architectures to move beyond learning the successor function to simulating the counting process more generally, and point towards a deeper understanding of what it means to understand the countably infinite.

papers.title: States Hidden in Hidden States: LLMs Emerge Discrete State Representations Implicitly
papers.research_question: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) form Implicit Discrete State Representations (IDSRs) during implicit consecutive addition tasks, and how are these representations formed and utilized?
papers.core_contribution: This paper discovers and analyzes Implicit Discrete State Representations (IDSRs) in LLMs, showing that models form and use these intermediate result representations to perform implicit consecutive addition without chain-of-thought.
papers.conclusion: LLMs form Implicit Discrete State Representations (IDSRs) to perform implicit consecutive addition, providing insight into their multi-step reasoning and state-tracking abilities.
papers.key_findings:
IDSRs exist in the hidden states of LLMs during consecutive addition tasks, as confirmed by probing experiments.
IDSRs are formed independently for each digit and sequentially from the least significant digit, mirroring human calculation order.
A layer-wise transition occurs: early layers (0-50) contain linear IDSRs, middle layers (50-65) transition from linear to non-linear, and later layers (65-79) have non-linear features.
IDSRs are propagated along the sequence and used for subsequent calculations, as demonstrated by an attention bridge experiment.
The resolution of IDSRs degrades with sequence length, leading to inaccuracies in current open-source models.
papers.limitation:
Task diversity is limited; the hypothesis is validated only on a synthetic dataset of mathematical formulas.
Model diversity is limited; interpretability analysis requires open-source models, so experiments primarily use Qwen-72b, which has a capability gap compared to SOTA closed-source models.
future_direction: Investigate influence factors (e.g., training data, CoT) on the resolution of generated IDSRs.
Explore the underlying causes of the dynamic changes in IDSR properties (formation interpretability).
Study the patterns of IDSR generation across different model scales (scalability).
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit various emergent abilities. Among these abilities, some might reveal the internal working mechanisms of models. In this paper, we uncover a novel emergent capability in models: the intrinsic ability to perform extended sequences of calculations without relying on chain-of-thought step-by-step solutions. Remarkably, the most advanced models can directly output the results of two-digit number additions with lengths extending up to 15 addends. We hypothesize that the model emerges Implicit Discrete State Representations (IDSRs) within its hidden states and performs symbolic calculations internally. To test this hypothesis, we design a sequence of experiments that look into the hidden states. Specifically, we first confirm that IDSRs exist. Then, we provide interesting observations about the formation of IDSRs from layer, digit, and sequence perspectives. Finally, we confirm that models indeed use IDSRs to produce the final answers. However, we also discover that these state representations are far from lossless in current open-sourced models, leading to inaccuracies in their final performance. Our work presents a novel exploration of LLMs' symbolic calculation abilities and the underlying mechanisms.

papers.title: The Impact of Positional Encoding on Length Generalization in Transformers
papers.research_question: What is the influence of positional encoding on length generalization in downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers without positional encoding (NoPE) outperform explicit positional encoding methods in length generalization on downstream tasks, without additional computation.
papers.conclusion: Explicit positional encodings are not essential for decoder-only Transformers to generalize well to longer sequences.
papers.key_findings:
NoPE outperforms all explicit positional encoding schemes on length generalization.
NoPE requires no additional computation in the attention mechanism.
NoPE can theoretically represent both absolute and relative positional encodings, but empirically it learns attention patterns similar to T5's Relative PE.
Scratchpad (chain-of-thought) is not always helpful for length generalization and its format highly impacts performance.
Commonly used positional encoding methods (ALiBi, Rotary, APE) are ill-suited for length generalization in downstream tasks.
papers.abstract: Length generalization, the ability to generalize from small training context sizes to larger ones, is a critical challenge in the development of Transformer-based language models. Positional encoding (PE) has been identified as a major factor influencing length generalization, but the exact impact of different PE schemes on extrapolation in downstream tasks remains unclear. In this paper, we conduct a systematic empirical study comparing the length generalization performance of decoder-only Transformers with five different position encoding approaches including Absolute Position Embedding (APE), T5's Relative PE, ALiBi, and Rotary, in addition to Transformers without positional encoding (NoPE). Our evaluation encompasses a battery of reasoning and mathematical tasks. Our findings reveal that the most commonly used positional encoding methods, such as ALiBi, Rotary, and APE, are not well suited for length generalization in downstream tasks. More importantly, NoPE outperforms other explicit positional encoding methods while requiring no additional computation. We theoretically demonstrate that NoPE can represent both absolute and relative PEs, but when trained with SGD, it mostly resembles T5's relative PE attention patterns. Finally, we find that scratchpad is not always helpful to solve length generalization and its format highly impacts the model's performance. Overall, our work suggests that explicit position embeddings are not essential for decoder-only Transformers to generalize well to longer sequences.

papers.title: Carrying over algorithm in transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformer models implement the carrying over algorithm for integer addition, and how are the tasks allocated to different network components?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that transformer models implement the carrying over algorithm for integer addition in a modular fashion, with specific layers handling digit addition, carry decision, and carry addition.
papers.conclusion: Transformers implement the carrying over algorithm in a modular way, and insights from small models can inform understanding of larger models and improve generalization.
papers.key_findings:
For two-layer encoder-only models, the carrying over algorithm is implemented modularly with the first layer adding digits, the second layer deciding where to carry, and the MLP adding the carried one.
The same implementation is found in three-layer and decoder-only models.
Suggestive evidence indicates similar mechanisms in large language models like Alpaca 7B, Llemma 7B, and Zephyr 7B.
Length generalization to larger digit sums can be achieved through priming or fine-tuning.
One-layer models exhibit a phase transition in attention patterns during training.
papers.limitation: The evidence for the implementation in large language models is suggestive and not conclusive.
future_direction: Exploring better prompting strategies for large language models
Studying stabilization of attention patterns for length generalization
papers.abstract: Addition is perhaps one of the simplest arithmetic tasks one can think of and is usually performed using the carrying over algorithm. This algorithm consists of two tasks: adding digits in the same position and carrying over a one whenever necessary. We study how transformer models implement this algorithm and how the two aforementioned tasks are allocated to different parts of the network. We first focus on two-layer encoder-only models and show that the carrying over algorithm is implemented in a modular fashion. The first layer is mostly responsible for adding digits in the same position. The second layer first decides, in the attention, which positions need a carried one or not, and then performs the carrying of the one in the final MLP. We provide a simple way of precisely identifying which neurons are responsible for that task. This implementation of the carrying over algorithm occurs across a range of hyperparameters for two as well as three-layer models. For small decoder-only models, we observe the same implementation and provide suggestive evidence for its existence in three 7B large language models.

papers.title: Transformer Feed-Forward Layers Are Key-Value Memories
papers.research_question: What is the function of feed-forward layers in transformer-based language models? The paper shows they operate as key-value memories.
papers.core_contribution: Feed-forward layers in transformer language models function as key-value memories, where keys capture input patterns and values represent output distributions, and the model's final output is constructed by composing and refining these memories across layers.
papers.conclusion: Feed-forward layers in transformers act as pattern-detecting key-value memories, and the model's output is gradually constructed by composing these memories within layers and refining them across layers via residual connections.
papers.key_findings:
Keys in feed-forward layers correlate with human-interpretable input patterns, with lower layers capturing shallow patterns (e.g., n-grams) and upper layers capturing semantic patterns.
Values in upper layers induce distributions over the output vocabulary that correlate with the next-token distribution of the patterns in the corresponding keys.
The output of a feed-forward layer is a composition of hundreds of active memories, rarely dominated by a single memory cell.
Residual connections act as a refinement mechanism, with the feed-forward layer often vetoing the residual's top prediction to shift probability mass to other candidates.
The model's final prediction is often determined in the lower layers, with upper layers refining the confidence and occasionally changing the prediction.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to one language model and dataset, and the assumption that all layers operate in the same embedding space may not hold for lower layers.
future_direction: Investigating the transformation of embedding spaces across layers and the interplay between feed-forward and self-attention layers.
Extending the analysis to other transformer models, such as BERT encoders and neural translation models.
Exploring practical implications for interpretability methods, data privacy (e.g., membership inference), and architectural innovations.
papers.abstract: Feed-forward layers constitute two-thirds of a transformer model's parameters, yet their role in the network remains under-explored. We show that feed-forward layers in transformerbased language models operate as key-value memories, where each key correlates with textual patterns in the training examples, and each value induces a distribution over the output vocabulary. Our experiments show that the learned patterns are human-interpretable, and that lower layers tend to capture shallow patterns, while upper layers learn more semantic ones. The values complement the keys' input patterns by inducing output distributions that concentrate probability mass on tokens likely to appear immediately after each pattern, particularly in the upper layers. Finally, we demonstrate that the output of a feed-forward layer is a composition of its memories, which is subsequently refined throughout the model's layers via residual connections to produce the final output distribution.

papers.title: Diagnostic Classifiers: Revealing how Neural Networks Process Hierarchical Structure
papers.research_question: How do neural networks process hierarchical structure, and what strategies do they use for compositional semantics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces diagnostic classifiers as a method to test hypotheses about the strategies neural networks use, and shows that a GRU follows an incremental strategy for processing hierarchical arithmetic expressions.
papers.conclusion: Diagnostic classifiers are a useful method for understanding how neural networks process hierarchical structure, and the GRU follows an incremental strategy for the arithmetic task.
papers.key_findings:
TreeRNNs can learn to compute the meaning of arithmetic expressions and generalize to longer expressions.
The TreeRNN solution can be understood geometrically through projection, summation, and squashing steps.
GRUs can also learn the task and generalize to longer expressions, but performance deteriorates with length and is worse for right-branching expressions.
Diagnostic classifiers reveal that the GRU follows an incremental strategy rather than a recursive one.
The diagnostic classifier method is a useful tool for analyzing neural network internal dynamics when visualization is insufficient.
papers.limitation:
The TreeRNN requires external parses and is not computationally efficient or biologically plausible.
The GRU's performance deteriorates with sentence length and is worse for right-branching sentences.
The diagnostic classifiers are linear and may not capture all information; the predictions change at every time step while target values remain the same, indicating a possible refinement.
papers.abstract: We investigate how neural networks can be used for hierarchical, compositional semantics. To this end, we define the simple but nontrivial artificial task of processing nested arithmetic expressions and study whether different types of neural networks can learn to add and subtract. We find that recursive neural networks can implement a generalising solution, and we visualise the intermediate steps: projection, summation and squashing. We also show that gated recurrent neural networks, which process the expressions incrementally, perform surprisingly well on this task: they learn to predict the outcome of the arithmetic expressions with reasonable accuracy, although performance deteriorates with increasing length. To analyse what strategy the recurrent network applies, visualisation techniques are less insightful. Therefore, we develop an approach where we formulate and test hypotheses on what strategies these networks might be following. For each hypothesis, we derive predictions about features of the hidden state representations at each time step, and train ’diagnostic classifiers’ to test those predictions. Our results indicate the networks follow a strategy similar to our hypothesised ’incremental strategy’.

papers.title: Finding Neurons in a Haystack: Case Studies with Sparse Probing
papers.research_question: How are high-level human-interpretable features represented within the internal neuron activations of LLMs, and how does the sparsity of these representations vary with model scale?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces sparse probing to localize individual neurons representing features in LLMs, revealing that early layers use superposition (sparse combinations of polysemantic neurons), middle layers have seemingly dedicated neurons for higher-level features, and model scale increases representational sparsity with varied dynamics.
papers.conclusion: Sparse probing is a powerful tool for understanding feature representation in LLMs, revealing superposition in early layers and monosemantic neurons in middle layers, with scaling effects on sparsity, and opens many directions for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Early layers represent many features in superposition via sparse linear combinations of polysemantic neurons.
Middle layers contain seemingly dedicated (monosemantic) neurons for higher-level contextual features like language or code.
Increasing model scale generally increases representational sparsity, but different features exhibit distinct scaling dynamics.
Sparse probing is an effective method for locating interpretable neurons, even when they are in superposition.
There is a tremendous amount of interpretable structure within the neurons of LLMs, accessible through careful probing and analysis.
papers.limitation:
Interpretation of neurons can be misleading due to 'interpretability illusions' from only examining maximum activating examples.
Conclusive statements about monosemanticity remain methodologically out of reach.
future_direction: Apply sparse probing to other model families and architectures.
Study the dynamics of feature representation during training, not just in final models.
Extend sparse probing to multimodal models and other modalities.
papers.abstract: Despite rapid adoption and deployment of large language models (LLMs), the internal computations of these models remain opaque and poorly understood. In this work, we seek to understand how high-level human-interpretable features are represented within the internal neuron activations of LLMs. We train $k$-sparse linear classifiers (probes) on these internal activations to predict the presence of features in the input; by varying the value of $k$ we study the sparsity of learned representations and how this varies with model scale. With $k=1$, we localize individual neurons which are highly relevant for a particular feature, and perform a number of case studies to illustrate general properties of LLMs. In particular, we show that early layers make use of sparse combinations of neurons to represent many features in superposition, that middle layers have seemingly dedicated neurons to represent higher-level contextual features, and that increasing scale causes representational sparsity to increase on average, but there are multiple types of scaling dynamics. In all, we probe for over 100 unique features comprising 10 different categories in 7 different models spanning 70 million to 6.9 billion parameters.

papers.title: How Post-Training Reshapes LLMs: A Mechanistic View on Knowledge, Truthfulness, Refusal, and Confidence
papers.research_question: How does post-training affect the internal mechanisms of large language models in terms of knowledge storage, truthfulness, refusal, and confidence?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a mechanistic analysis of how post-training affects LLMs internally, revealing which mechanisms are preserved (e.g., knowledge storage locations, truthfulness direction) and which are altered (e.g., refusal direction), with implications for model steering and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Post-training preserves some internal mechanisms (like knowledge storage and truthfulness direction) and alters others (like refusal direction), providing insights for model steering and future research in interpretability and LLM post-training.
papers.key_findings:
Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations in LLMs.
Post-training adapts knowledge representations from the base model while also developing new ones.
The truthfulness direction is highly similar between base and post-trained models and is effectively transferable for interventions.
The refusal direction differs between base and post-trained models and shows limited forward transferability.
Differences in confidence between base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons.
papers.limitation: Complex, multi-step processes such as reasoning and instruction-following are not well-captured by current mechanistic interpretability tools, limiting the scope of analysis.
future_direction: Design better post-training methods based on mechanistic insights.
Extend analysis to other capabilities like reasoning and instruction-following.
papers.abstract: Post-training is essential for the success of large language models (LLMs), transforming pre-trained base models into more useful and aligned post-trained models. While plenty of works have studied post-training algorithms and evaluated post-training models by their outputs, it remains understudied how post-training reshapes LLMs internally. In this paper, we compare base and post-trained LLMs mechanistically from four perspectives to better understand post-training effects. Our findings across model families and datasets reveal that: (1) Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations, and it adapts knowledge representations from the base model while developing new knowledge representations; (2) Both truthfulness and refusal can be represented by vectors in the hidden representation space. The truthfulness direction is highly similar between the base and post-trained model, and it is effectively transferable for interventions; (3) The refusal direction is different between the base and post-trained models, and it shows limited forward transferability; (4) Differences in confidence between the base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons. Our study provides insights into the fundamental mechanisms preserved and altered during post-training, facilitates downstream tasks like model steering, and could potentially benefit future research in interpretability and LLM post-training. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/HZD01/post-training-mechanistic-analysis.

papers.title: The Representation and Recall of Interwoven Structured Knowledge in LLMs: A Geometric and Layered Analysis
papers.research_question: How do LLMs encode interwoven scientific knowledge, and do they reflect geometric structures like the periodic table?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode scientific knowledge in geometric structures, such as a 3D spiral aligning with the periodic table, representing knowledge as interwoven manifolds rather than isolated facts.
papers.conclusion: LLMs develop internal representations that reflect the structured geometry of scientific knowledge, representing symbolic knowledge as geometry-aware, interwoven manifolds.
papers.key_findings:
A 3D spiral structure is observed in hidden states that aligns with the periodic table.
Middle layers encode continuous attributes enabling indirect recall, while deeper layers sharpen categorical distinctions.
Linguistic context increasingly shapes representations in later layers.
Middle layers have strong linear associations between related attributes, which weaken in deeper layers.
papers.limitation:
Prompts are focused on chemical elements and may not extend to domains with more abstract features.
Hypothesis-driven validation may oversimplify LLMs' non-linear interactions.
future_direction: Further investigation into how LLMs represent and reason about scientific knowledge, such as materials property prediction.
Informing the design of downstream embedding-based tasks.
papers.abstract: This study investigates how large language models (LLMs) represent and recall multi-associated attributes across transformer layers. We show that intermediate layers encode factual knowledge by superimposing related attributes in overlapping spaces, along with effective recall even when attributes are not explicitly prompted. In contrast, later layers refine linguistic patterns and progressively separate attribute representations, optimizing task-specific outputs while appropriately narrowing attribute recall. We identify diverse encoding patterns including, for the first time, the observation of 3D spiral structures when exploring information related to the periodic table of elements. Our findings reveal a dynamic transition in attribute representations across layers, contributing to mechanistic interpretability and providing insights for understanding how LLMs handle complex, interrelated knowledge.

papers.title: Factual Probing Is [MASK]: Learning vs. Learning to Recall
papers.research_question: Can we interpret factual probing results as a lower bound on the factual information encoded in a language model, or do prompt-search methods learn from the training data?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces OPTI PROMPT, a continuous prompt optimization method that improves factual probing accuracy, and shows that optimized prompts can exploit regularities in training data, complicating the interpretation of probing results.
papers.conclusion: OPTI PROMPT is an effective method for factual probing, but data-driven prompt optimization can exploit training data regularities, making it challenging to interpret probing results as a pure lower bound on model knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
OPTI PROMPT improves top-1 accuracy on the LAMA benchmark by 6.4% over previous methods.
Training data for factual probing contains regularities (e.g., class priors, lexical correlations) that can be exploited by prompt optimization methods.
Optimized prompts can predict facts even when probing randomly initialized models, indicating they learn from training data rather than solely eliciting stored knowledge.
Partitioning test facts into 'easy' (predictable from training data) and 'hard' subsets reveals that OPTI PROMPT improves on both, suggesting it is better at learning from data and eliciting facts from the language model.
Continuous prompt optimization is more efficient and effective than discrete token search, but requires white-box model access.
papers.limitation:
It is difficult to determine whether a prediction comes from the language model's stored knowledge or from patterns learned from the training data during prompt optimization.
Gradient-based prompt optimization methods like OPTI PROMPT require white-box access to the model, limiting their use with API-based large models.
future_direction: Develop techniques for attributing predictions to specific training instances to better understand the source of factual knowledge.
Pursue more mechanistic explanations for how language models learn and represent factual information, beyond prompt-based probing.
papers.abstract: demonstrated that it is possible to retrieve world facts from a pretrained language model by expressing them as cloze-style prompts and interpret the model's prediction accuracy as a lower bound on the amount of factual information it encodes. Subsequent work has attempted to tighten the estimate by searching for better prompts, using a disjoint set of facts as training data. In this work, we make two complementary contributions to better understand these factual probing techniques. First, we propose OPTIPROMPT, a novel and efficient method which directly optimizes in continuous embedding space. We find this simple method is able to predict an additional 6.4% of facts in the LAMA benchmark. Second, we raise a more important question: Can we really interpret these probing results as a lower bound? Is it possible that these prompt-search methods learn from the training data too? We find, somewhat surprisingly, that the training data used by these methods contains certain regularities of the underlying fact distribution, and all the existing prompt methods, including ours, are able to exploit them for better fact prediction. We conduct a set of control experiments to disentangle "learning" from "learning to recall", providing a more detailed picture of what different prompts can reveal about pre-trained language models.

papers.title: Calibrating LLM Confidence by Probing Perturbed Representation Stability
papers.research_question: How can we improve LLM confidence estimation by analyzing the stability of internal representations under targeted adversarial perturbations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CCPS, a method that estimates LLM confidence by analyzing the stability of internal representations under adversarial perturbations, achieving significant improvements in calibration and discrimination metrics across diverse models and benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CCPS provides an efficient, accurate, and generalizable method for LLM confidence estimation, enhancing the trustworthiness of LLMs in critical domains.
papers.key_findings:
CCPS reduces average Expected Calibration Error by approximately 55% (up to 88%) and Brier score by 21% (up to 45%) compared to the best baseline.
CCPS increases average Accuracy by 5 percentage points, AUCPR by 4 percentage points, and AUROC by 6 percentage points.
CCPS generalizes across diverse LLM architectures (Llama, Qwen, Mistral) and model scales (8B to 32B parameters).
CCPS performs well on both multiple-choice and open-ended question answering formats.
CCPS is parameter-efficient, adding only around 9.5k trainable parameters, compared to baselines that may add millions.
papers.abstract: Reza Khanmohammadi, Erfan Miahi, Mehrsa Mardikoraem, Simerjot Kaur, Ivan Brugere, Charese Smiley, Kundan S Thind, Mohammad M. Ghassemi. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing. 2025.

papers.title: Steering Risk Preferences in Large Language Models by Aligning Behavioral and Neural Representations
papers.research_question: How can steering vectors be systematically identified to change LLM behavior? The paper proposes a principled approach by aligning latent representations from behavioral methods (Markov chain Monte Carlo with LLMs) with neural counterparts.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method for deriving steering vectors by aligning behavioral representations (elicited via MCMC with LLMs) with neural activations, enabling precise control of LLM risk preferences without retraining.
papers.conclusion: Self-alignment methods that align behavioral and neural representations offer an effective and principled means of controlling LLM behavior in risk-sensitive contexts.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors derived from aligned behavioral and neural representations (MCMC and Certainty Equivalent methods) outperform Contrastive Activation in steering risky decisions, risk perception, and text generation.
The optimal layer for steering varies: risk perception is more steerable in earlier layers, while risky decisions are more steerable in later layers.
The method allows precise control over risk preferences (risk-seeking vs. risk-averse) across different tasks.
Steering vectors transfer to tasks far from the original elicitation context.
The behavioral representation from MCMC reveals more nuanced risk preferences compared to the Certainty Equivalent method.
papers.limitation:
Further theoretical and mechanistic interpretability research is needed to establish a more concrete link between behaviorally elicited representations and their corresponding neural activations.
Modifying a Transformer’s residual stream is not uniformly effective across all layers; the success of such interventions is highly dependent on the layer selected. Identifying optimal layers for steering remains an open question.
This form of steering is limited in scope for proprietary models where weights are not accessible, restricting its broader applicability.
future_direction: Identifying optimal layers for steering remains an open question for future research.
Future research should consider developing new descriptive frameworks tailored to characterizing and predicting the risky choices of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Changing the behavior of large language models (LLMs) can be as straightforward as editing the Transformer's residual streams using appropriately constructed "steering vectors." These modifications to internal neural activations, a form of representation engineering, offer an effective and targeted means of influencing model behavior without retraining or fine-tuning the model. But how can such steering vectors be systematically identified? We propose a principled approach for uncovering steering vectors by aligning latent representations elicited through behavioral methods (specifically, Markov chain Monte Carlo with LLMs) with their neural counterparts. To evaluate this approach, we focus on extracting latent risk preferences from LLMs and steering their risk-related outputs using the aligned representations as steering vectors. We show that the resulting steering vectors successfully and reliably modulate LLM outputs in line with the targeted behavior.

papers.title: Exploring the Role of BERT Token Representations to Explain Sentence Probing Results
papers.research_question: What role do specific token representations play in BERT's ability to encode linguistic features and explain probing results?
papers.core_contribution: BERT encodes linguistic features in specific token representations, and gradient-based attribution can reveal these subspaces to explain probing performance.
papers.conclusion: BERT's token representations encode specific linguistic knowledge, and attribution methods provide insights into probing results, revealing distinct subspaces for different features.
papers.key_findings:
Sentence-ending tokens retain positional information in higher layers.
The ##s token encodes both noun number and verb tense information, and BERT separates these usages into distinct subspaces.
In bi-gram shift tasks, inverted tokens have higher attribution scores, and abnormalities are encoded in their representations.
In coordination inversion, coordinators like 'and' and 'but' play a key role, and their representations change significantly.
Attribution patterns are consistent even with less training data, indicating that knowledge is well-encoded in representations.
future_direction: Investigate how subspaces evolve during fine-tuning
Check if behaviors are affected by different training objectives
Use token-level analysis for model efficiency
papers.abstract: Several studies have been carried out on revealing linguistic features captured by BERT. This is usually achieved by training a diagnostic classifier on the representations obtained from different layers of BERT. The subsequent classification accuracy is then interpreted as the ability of the model in encoding the corresponding linguistic property. Despite providing insights, these studies have left out the potential role of token representations. In this paper, we provide a more in-depth analysis on the representation space of BERT in search for distinct and meaningful subspaces that can explain the reasons behind these probing results. Based on a set of probing tasks and with the help of attribution methods we show that BERT tends to encode meaningful knowledge in specific token representations (which are often ignored in standard classification setups), allowing the model to detect syntactic and semantic abnormalities, and to distinctively separate grammatical number and tense subspaces. 1

papers.title: Why transformers are obviously good models of language
papers.research_question: Why are transformers effective models of language, and how do they align with theoretical perspectives on language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that transformers are good models of language because their architecture, such as word embeddings and attention mechanisms, aligns with cognitive linguistic theories like prototype theory and construction grammar.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are effective models of language, and their alignment with certain linguistic theories suggests that these theories, such as those from cognitive linguistics, are correct.
papers.key_findings:
Word embeddings in transformers represent prototypical meanings of words, similar to Rosch's prototype theory.
Contextualized word meanings are constructed through self-attention layers, updating prototypes based on context.
Transformers can handle syntax and top-down processing via attention heads and skip connections, analogous to construction grammar.
Transformers lack a bias for local dependencies, allowing them to learn rare long-distance dependencies effectively.
The empirical success of transformers supports cognitive linguistic approaches over traditional syntactic theories.
papers.limitation:
Transformers assert false facts with the same degree of authority as true information.
Transformers have myopia in social contexts, such as not remembering past interactions in chatbots.
papers.abstract: Nobody knows how language works, but many theories abound. Transformers are a class of neural networks that process language automatically with more success than alternatives, both those based on neural computations and those that rely on other (e.g. more symbolic) mechanisms. Here, I highlight direct connections between the transformer architecture and certain theoretical perspectives on language. The empirical success of transformers relative to alternative models provides circumstantial evidence that the linguistic approaches that transformers embody should be, at least, evaluated with greater scrutiny by the linguistics community and, at best, considered to be the currently best available theories.

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
papers.research_question: Are some language model representations inherently multi-dimensional, and if so, how are these irreducible multi-dimensional features used in computation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that language models learn irreducible multi-dimensional features (e.g., circular representations for days of the week and months of the year) and provides evidence that these features are the fundamental unit of computation for modular arithmetic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary for a complete mechanistic decomposition of some language model behaviors, challenging the strict one-dimensional linear representation hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can automatically discover interpretable multi-dimensional features in language models, such as circular representations for days of the week and months of the year.
These circular features are irreducible according to formal separability and mixture indices, meaning they cannot be decomposed into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features.
Models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B use these exact circular representations when solving modular arithmetic problems involving days and months.
Intervention experiments (subspace patching) show that the circular representations are causally involved in the model's computation for these tasks.
The circular representations respect a continuous notion of time, as shown by interventions with phrases like 'early Monday' and 'late Monday'.
papers.abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.

papers.title: In-Context Algebra
papers.research_question: What computational strategies do transformers develop when tokens serve as pure variables, acquiring meaning only through their interactions within each sequence, rather than relying on fixed information encoded in token embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers trained on an in-context variable assignment task develop symbolic reasoning mechanisms (commutative copying, identity element recognition, closure-based cancellation) that differ from the geometric representations learned in fixed-token arithmetic settings, showing that learned reasoning strategies depend on task structure.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can develop symbolic reasoning mechanisms when trained to reason in-context about variables whose meanings are not fixed, showing that the kinds of learned strategies are dependent on the task structure.
papers.key_findings:
Models learn a commutative copying mechanism where a dedicated attention head copies answers from previously seen commutative facts.
Models develop an identity element recognition mechanism that distinguishes and solves facts containing the group's identity element.
Models implement a closure-based cancellation mechanism that tracks group membership to constrain valid answers by eliminating impossible variables.
The reasoning strategies learned by transformers are dependent on the task structure, with symbolic, context-based strategies emerging when tokens carry no consistent meaning across contexts.
Models achieve near-perfect accuracy on the task and generalize to unseen groups.
papers.limitation: The study is conducted on synthetic algebra tasks with small transformer models, which may limit generalizability to larger models or more complex, real-world reasoning tasks.
future_direction: Exploring more complex algebraic structures and reasoning tasks.
Scaling the analysis to larger transformer models.
Investigating whether similar symbolic mechanisms emerge in other in-context learning settings.
papers.abstract: We investigate the mechanisms that arise when transformers are trained to solve arithmetic on sequences where tokens are variables whose meaning is determined only through their interactions. While prior work has found that transformers develop geometric embeddings that mirror algebraic structure, those previous findings emerge from settings where arithmetic-valued tokens have fixed meanings. We devise a new task in which the assignment of symbols to specific algebraic group elements varies from one sequence to another. Despite this challenging setup, transformers achieve near-perfect accuracy on the task and even generalize to unseen algebraic groups. We develop targeted data distributions to create causal tests of a set of hypothesized mechanisms, and we isolate three mechanisms models consistently learn: commutative copying where a dedicated head copies answers, identity element recognition that distinguishes identity-containing facts, and closure-based cancellation that tracks group membership to constrain valid answers. Complementary to the geometric representations found in fixed-symbol settings, our findings show that models develop symbolic reasoning mechanisms when trained to reason in-context with variables whose meanings are not fixed.

papers.title: A Causal Framework to Quantify the Robustness of Mathematical Reasoning with Language Models
papers.research_question: How robust is the mathematical reasoning of language models on math word problems, and what are the causal effects of input factors (e.g., surface form, operands, operators) on the model's solution?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a causal framework to quantify the robustness and sensitivity of language models on math word problems, finding that GPT-3 Davinci models show dramatic improvement in both aspects compared to other GPT variants.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a causal framework for behavioral analysis of language models on math word problems, revealing that robustness does not continuously improve with size, but GPT-3 Davinci models show significant improvement, though performance degrades on more complex problems.
papers.key_findings:
Larger non-instruction-tuned models tend to be more sensitive to changes in the ground-truth result, but not necessarily more robust.
GPT-3 Davinci models (175B) achieve a dramatic improvement in both robustness and sensitivity compared to all other GPT variants.
Instruction tuning (as in GPT-3 Davinci) improves robustness and sensitivity, but the type of instruction tuning matters.
For three-operand problems, even the best models (GPT-3 Davinci) show a significant degradation in robustness.
The causal framework allows disentangling the direct and total causal effects of operands (N) and textual surface form (S) on model predictions.
papers.limitation:
The numerical space for operands is limited to integers up to 300 to ensure numbers are represented as single tokens.
For GPT-3, the API only returns top-k logits, so causal effect metrics (δrcc) are approximated.
The LLaMA tokenizer treats each digit as a separate token, making probability comparison for multi-digit numbers problematic.
future_direction: Examine different types of instruction tuning (e.g., focused on reasoning procedures or reinforcement learning from human feedback).
Extend the framework to more complex problems (e.g., with more operands or different types of math problems).
papers.abstract: We have recently witnessed a number of impressive results on hard mathematical reasoning problems with language models. At the same time, the robustness of these models has also been called into question; recent works have shown that models can rely on shallow patterns in the problem description when generating a solution. Building on the idea of behavioral testing, we propose a novel framework, which pins down the causal effect of various factors in the input, e.g., the surface form of the problem text, the operands, and math operators on the output solution. By grounding the behavioral analysis in a causal graph describing an intuitive reasoning process, we study the behavior of language models in terms of robustness and sensitivity to direct interventions in the input space. We apply our framework on a test bed of math word problems. Our analysis shows that robustness does not appear to continuously improve as a function of size, but the GPT-3 Davinci models (175B) achieve a dramatic improvement in both robustness and sensitivity compared to all other GPT variants.

papers.title: Emotions Where Art Thou: Understanding and Characterizing the Emotional Latent Space of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models (LLMs) internally represent emotion by analyzing the geometry of their hidden-state space?
papers.core_contribution: This work reveals a consistent and manipulable affective geometry in LLMs, showing that emotional representations form a low-dimensional, directionally encoded subspace that generalizes across datasets and languages, and can be steered via targeted interventions.
papers.conclusion: The findings reveal a consistent and manipulable affective geometry in LLMs and offer insight into how they internalize and process emotion.
papers.key_findings:
A low-dimensional emotional manifold exists in LLMs, with emotional representations being directionally encoded, distributed across layers, and aligned with interpretable dimensions.
The emotional structure is stable across depth and generalizes to eight real-world emotion datasets spanning five languages.
Cross-domain alignment yields low error and strong linear probe performance, indicating a universal emotional subspace.
Internal emotion perception can be steered while preserving semantics using a learned intervention module, with especially strong control for basic emotions across languages.
Emotional information is not localized but distributed broadly and redundantly throughout the network, with high separability emerging from overlapping, multi-purpose components.
papers.limitation: The steering technique does not uniformly override model behavior but respects representational limits, with variability in steerability across languages and domains (e.g., low-resource or archaic corpora) functioning as an inherent boundary.
papers.abstract: This work investigates how large language models (LLMs) internally represent emotion by analyzing the geometry of their hidden-state space. The paper identifies a low-dimensional emotional manifold and shows that emotional representations are directionally encoded, distributed across layers, and aligned with interpretable dimensions. These structures are stable across depth and generalize to eight real-world emotion datasets spanning five languages. Cross-domain alignment yields low error and strong linear probe performance, indicating a universal emotional subspace. Within this space, internal emotion perception can be steered while preserving semantics using a learned intervention module, with especially strong control for basic emotions across languages. These findings reveal a consistent and manipulable affective geometry in LLMs and offer insight into how they internalize and process emotion.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Analogies: Investigating Analogical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode and apply high-level relational concepts for analogical reasoning, and how do they structurally align analogous situations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates the internal mechanisms of analogical reasoning in LLMs, finding that they encode relational information in mid-upper layers but struggle to apply it, and that successful reasoning is associated with strong structural alignment between analogous situations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs show emerging but limited capabilities in analogical reasoning, with parallels to human cognition in encoding relational information and structural alignment, but gaps in application and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs effectively encode underlying relationships between analogous entities in mid-upper layers, with relational information being a key factor for correct reasoning.
LLMs struggle not only when relational information is missing but also when attempting to apply it to new entities.
Strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer and improve performance.
Successful analogical reasoning is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, while failures show degraded alignment.
Analogical structure becomes linearly separable in middle layers, and token-level alignment (measured by Mutual Alignment Score) is higher for correct analogies.
future_direction: Future research into understanding and improving the analogical reasoning capabilities of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Analogical reasoning is at the core of human cognition, serving as an important foundation for a variety of intellectual activities. While prior work has shown that LLMs can represent task patterns and surface-level concepts, it remains unclear whether these models can encode high-level relational concepts and apply them to novel situations through structured comparisons. In this work, we explore this fundamental aspect using proportional and story analogies, and identify three key findings. First, LLMs effectively encode the underlying relationships between analogous entities; both attributive and relational information propagate through mid-upper layers in correct cases, whereas reasoning failures reflect missing relational information within these layers. Second, unlike humans, LLMs often struggle not only when relational information is missing, but also when attempting to apply it to new entities. In such cases, strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer to a certain extent. Lastly, successful analogical reasoning in LLMs is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, whereas failures often reflect degraded or misplaced alignment. Overall, our findings reveal that LLMs exhibit emerging but limited capabilities in encoding and applying high-level relational concepts, highlighting both parallels and gaps with human cognition.

papers.title: Under the Hood: Using Diagnostic Classifiers to Investigate and Improve how Language Models Track Agreement Information
papers.research_question: How do neural language models keep track of number agreement between subject and verb?
papers.core_contribution: Diagnostic classifiers provide a detailed understanding of how LSTM language models represent subject-verb agreement information, and this understanding can be used to intervene and improve model performance on agreement tasks.
papers.conclusion: Diagnostic classifiers offer a detailed understanding of where and when information is encoded in a neural model, and this information can be used post hoc to change the course of processing.
papers.key_findings:
Number information is encoded dynamically over time, with a stable 'deep' representation maintained between subject and verb.
For sentences where the model makes agreement errors, the number information is already corrupted at the subject timestep.
The memory cell and hidden activation in the second layer are most specialized for processing number information.
Intervention using diagnostic classifiers at the subject timestep significantly improves the model's agreement accuracy.
papers.abstract: How do neural language models keep track of number agreement between subject and verb? We show that 'diagnostic classifiers', trained to predict number from the internal states of a language model, provide a detailed understanding of how, when, and where this information is represented. Moreover, they give us insight into when and where number information is corrupted in cases where the language model ends up making agreement errors. To demonstrate the causal role played by the representations we find, we then use agreement information to influence the course of the LSTM during the processing of difficult sentences. Results from such an intervention reveal a large increase in the language model's accuracy. Together, these results show that diagnostic classifiers give us an unrivalled detailed look into the representation of linguistic information in neural models, and demonstrate that this knowledge can be used to improve their performance.

papers.title: Inspecting and Editing Knowledge Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we map natural language statements to fact encodings in an LM's internal representations to enable editing and probing of knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: REMEDI is a method that learns to map natural language statements to fact encodings in LM representations, enabling both editing of knowledge (by adding vectors to hidden representations) and probing of existing knowledge.
papers.conclusion: REMEDI links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.
papers.key_findings:
REMEDI can patch errors made by an LM and insert new facts with or without context provided in the prompt.
REMEDI can help detect errors before generation by comparing edit vectors to unedited representations.
REMEDI increases accuracy on occupation classification and factual editing tasks compared to prompting baselines.
REMEDI generalizes from out-of-context training to in-context editing, suggesting unified representation of background and contextual knowledge.
REMEDI edits preserve correlations between features (e.g., adding 'made of metal' increases probability of 'shiny').
papers.limitation:
REMEDI can occasionally lead to disfluent or incorrect generations.
REMEDI sometimes damages the essence of the entity (e.g., making Wiener schnitzel an anime instead of a food).
REMEDI can also cause unrelated facts to change (e.g., changing the air dates of a TV show).
future_direction: Developing controlled generation interfaces that allow direct steering of model behavior in representation space.
Building tools for monitoring and controlling language generation by directly specifying facts and situations in an LM's native encoding scheme.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) represent facts about the world described by text. Sometimes these facts derive from training data (in most LMs, a representation of the word "banana" encodes the fact that bananas are fruits). Sometimes facts derive from input text itself (a representation of the sentence "I poured out the bottle" encodes the fact that the bottle became empty). We describe REMEDI, a method for learning to map statements in natural language to fact encodings in an LM's internal representation system. REMEDI encodings can be used as knowledge editors: when added to LM hidden representations, they modify downstream generation to be consistent with new facts. REMEDI encodings may also be used as probes: when compared to LM representations, they reveal which properties LMs already attribute to mentioned entities, in some cases making it possible to predict when LMs will generate outputs that conflict with background knowledge or input text. REMEDI thus links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.

papers.title: Can LLMs Predict Their Own Failures? Self-Awareness via Internal Circuits
papers.research_question: Can LLMs predict their own failures by inspecting internal states during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Gnosis, a lightweight self-awareness mechanism that enables frozen LLMs to perform intrinsic self-verification by decoding signals from hidden states and attention patterns with negligible inference overhead.
papers.conclusion: Gnosis provides a highly efficient framework for self-evaluation and sibling modeling, enabling early error detection and compute-aware control, demonstrating that intrinsic self-verification is both scalable and cost-effective.
papers.key_findings:
Gnosis consistently outperforms strong internal baselines and large external judges (e.g., 8B reward models, Gemini 2.5 Pro) in accuracy and calibration across math reasoning, QA, and academic knowledge benchmarks.
Gnosis generalizes zero-shot to partial generations, enabling early detection of failing trajectories and compute-aware control.
A Gnosis head trained on a small backbone transfers effectively to judge larger sibling models without fine-tuning.
Gnosis adds only ~5M parameters and operates with negligible inference cost, independent of sequence length.
Results show that reliable correctness cues are intrinsic to the generation process and can be extracted efficiently without external supervision.
papers.limitation: Gnosis is designed as a self-awareness mechanism rather than a general-purpose reward model; it transfers robustly to siblings but is not capable of acting as a general reward model.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) generate fluent and complex outputs but often fail to recognize their own mistakes and hallucinations. Existing approaches typically rely on external judges, multi-sample consistency, or text-based self-critique, which incur additional compute or correlate weakly with true correctness. We ask: can LLMs predict their own failures by inspecting internal states during inference? We introduce Gnosis, a lightweight self-awareness mechanism that enables frozen LLMs to perform intrinsic self-verification by decoding signals from hidden states and attention patterns. Gnosis passively observes internal traces, compresses them into fixed-budget descriptors, and predicts correctness with negligible inference cost, adding only ~5M parameters and operating independently of sequence length.
