papers.research_question: Why do generative transformer models exhibit strong in-distribution generalization but poor out-of-distribution generalization on arithmetic tasks, and is there a systematic pattern behind the OOD failures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that generative transformer models trained on n-digit arithmetic operations learn to map out-of-distribution inputs to outputs via equivalence classes modulo 10^n, explaining their poor OOD performance as systematic rather than random errors.
papers.conclusion: Generative transformer models exhibit equivalence generalization, mapping OOD inputs to ID equivalence classes, and representation learning plays a crucial role in both ID and OOD generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Models achieve near-perfect ID generalization but zero OOD accuracy on longer-digit arithmetic tasks.
The models learn an algebraic structure: they map OOD inputs to outputs by taking the operands modulo 10^n (for n-digit training), a phenomenon termed equivalence generalization.
Equivalence generalization is robust across different encoding methods, training data variations, and model scales.
Representation learning evolves from random to structured, enabling ID generalization but leading to systematic errors in OOD.
Increasing model size does not improve length generalization ability.
papers.limitation: The findings are based on synthetic arithmetic tasks and may not directly translate to natural language tasks due to the subjectivity and complexity of language.
future_direction: Using equivalence generalization as prior knowledge to guide training and reduce data needs
Applying equivalence class similarity metrics to domain adaptation for OOD generalization
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable proficiency on solving diverse problems. However, their generalization ability is not always satisfying and the generalization problem is common for generative transformer models in general. Researchers take basic mathematical tasks like n-digit addition or multiplication as important perspectives for investigating their generalization behaviors. It is observed that when training models on n-digit operations (e.g., additions) in which both input operands are n-digit in length, models generalize successfully on unseen n-digit inputs (in-distribution (ID) generalization), but fail miserably on longer, unseen cases (out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization). We bring this unexplained performance drop into attention and ask whether there is systematic OOD generalization. Towards understanding LLMs, we train various smaller language models which may share the same underlying mechanism. We discover that the strong ID generalization stems from structured representations, while behind the unsatisfying OOD performance, the models still exhibit clear learned algebraic structures. Specifically, these models map unseen OOD inputs to outputs with learned equivalence relations in the ID domain, which we call the equivalence generalization. These findings deepen our knowledge regarding the generalizability of generative models including LLMs, and provide insights into potential avenues for improvement.

papers.title: Emergence of a High-Dimensional Abstraction Phase in Language Transformers
papers.research_question: What does the evolution of intrinsic dimension (ID) over layers reveal about representational generalizability and linguistic processing in language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers a distinct high-dimensionality phase in the intermediate layers of language transformers, which corresponds to the first full linguistic abstraction of the input and is predictive of model performance.
papers.conclusion: Different LMs consistently develop a central-layer phase where the intrinsic dimension is expanded, which is the locus of deeper linguistic processing.
papers.key_findings:
A distinct phase characterized by a peak in the intrinsic dimension of representations emerges in intermediate layers across five transformer-based LMs.
This high-ID phase is significantly reduced with random text and absent in untrained models, indicating it reflects learned linguistic structure.
The layer at which the ID peak appears correlates with language modeling quality.
The highest-dimensional representations of different networks predict each other, suggesting they encode similar abstract information.
The ID peak marks a transition from surface-form to syntactic and semantic processing, and representations within it are the first to viably transfer to downstream tasks.
papers.limitation: The paper focuses on detecting broad qualitative patterns; future work should establish a clearer causal connection between intrinsic dimension and language processing via layer ablation studies.
future_direction: Establish causal connection via layer ablations and constraining dimensionality during processing.
Test the effect of pruning inside and outside the ID peak.
Study the relation between the ID profile and specific circuits detected in mechanistic interpretability work.
Use ID profiles for model pruning, fine-tuning, model stitching, and brain encoding models.
papers.abstract: A language model (LM) is a mapping from a linguistic context to an output token. However, much remains to be known about this mapping, including how its geometric properties relate to its function. We take a high-level geometric approach to its analysis, observing, across five pre-trained transformer-based LMs and three input datasets, a distinct phase characterized by high intrinsic dimensionality. During this phase, representations (1) correspond to the first full linguistic abstraction of the input; (2) are the first to viably transfer to downstream tasks; (3) predict each other across different LMs. Moreover, we find that an earlier onset of the phase strongly predicts better language modelling performance. In short, our results suggest that a central high-dimensionality phase underlies core linguistic processing in many common LM architectures.

papers.title: Linguistic generalization and compositionality in modern artificial neural networks
papers.research_question: How do modern deep artificial neural networks achieve linguistic generalization and productivity, and do they rely on systematic compositional rules?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reviews evidence that modern deep neural networks can achieve sophisticated linguistic generalization without relying on systematic compositional rules, and argues this behavior offers a new perspective on computational strategies for linguistic productivity relevant to cognitive science.
papers.conclusion: Modern deep neural networks are proficient at language processing and exhibit subtle grammatical generalization, yet they do not rely on systematic compositional rules, offering a comparative perspective for studying linguistic productivity and non-systematic generalization patterns in human language.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks can capture abstract, structure-dependent grammatical generalizations (e.g., long-distance number agreement) even in nonsensical sentences.
These networks fail at systematic compositional generalization in controlled tasks like the SCAN benchmark (e.g., jump and around-right splits).
Some architectures (e.g., convolutional seq2seq) show partial success on compositional splits but without systematicity, making errors uniformly across composition frames.
In communication games, neural networks can develop productive but non-compositional codes that generalize as well as compositional ones.
Analysis of a network's internal circuitry (e.g., ablation studies) suggests it develops genuine grammatical processing mechanisms rather than relying on surface heuristics.
papers.limitation: Our current understanding of the strategies learned by these networks is very limited, and better analytical tools are needed to uncover the mechanisms behind the dissociation of productive grammatical competence and systematic compositionality.
future_direction: Develop better analytical tools to uncover the mechanisms that lead to the detected dissociation of productive grammatical competence and systematic compositionality.

Investigate whether making neural networks more compositional, for example by means of more structured modular architectures, will make them more adaptive and faster at learning without sacrificing generality.

Use progress in understanding the linguistic capabilities of neural networks to make precise predictions about the origin, scope, and mechanics of non-systematic productive phenomena in human language.
papers.abstract: In the last decade, deep artificial neural networks have achieved astounding performance in many natural language-processing tasks. Given the high productivity of language, these models must possess effective generalization abilities. It is widely assumed that humans handle linguistic productivity by means of algebraic compositional rules: are deep networks similarly compositional? After reviewing the main innovations characterizing current deep language-processing networks, I discuss a set of studies suggesting that deep networks are capable of subtle grammar-dependent generalizations, but also that they do not rely on systematic compositional rules. I argue that the intriguing behaviour of these devices (still awaiting a full understanding) should be of interest to linguists and cognitive scientists, as it offers a new perspective on possible computational strategies to deal with linguistic productivity beyond rule-based compositionality, and it might lead to new insights into the less systematic generalization patterns that also appear in natural language. This article is part of the theme issue 'Towards mechanistic models of meaning composition'.

papers.title: Interventional Probing in High Dimensions: An NLI Case Study
papers.research_question: What are the limitations of amnesic probing in high-dimensional, low-class-count settings, and can an alternative method (mnestic probing) provide more informative results?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces mnestic probing, a variation of interventional probing that keeps only probe-selected directions, and shows it is more informative than amnesic probing in high-dimensional, low-class-count settings.
papers.conclusion: Mnestic probing provides more informative results than amnesic probing in high-dimensional, low-class-count settings, and amnesic probing may lead to incorrect conclusions about feature importance.
papers.key_findings:
Amnesic probing can be misleading in high-dimensional settings because removing a small number of probe-selected directions may not affect downstream performance due to redundancy.
Mnestic probing, which keeps only probe-selected directions, shows a more structured increase in downstream performance compared to random baselines.
In the natural logic setting, amnesic probing fails to show the expected effect of semantic features on NLI classification, while mnestic probing does.
The number of label classes (and thus removed directions) in amnesic probing is too small to observe an impact on downstream performance in high-dimensional representations.
Random control baselines for amnesic probing are not reliable because random removal of directions can have variable effects.
papers.limitation:
Mnestic probing results must be compared to random baselines because adding dimensions naturally increases information.
Linear probes may miss non-linearly encoded information, and the final linear classification layer cannot exploit such information.
Probe-selected subspaces may include correlated features, which must be considered when drawing conclusions.
future_direction: Analyze the dot products between random directions and probe-selected directions to check for alignment.
Investigate whether high performance in random control directions corresponds to strong alignment with probe-selected directions.
papers.abstract: Probing strategies have been shown to detect the presence of various linguistic features in large language models; in particular, semantic features intermediate to the "natural logic" fragment of the Natural Language Inference task (NLI). In the case of natural logic, the relation between the intermediate features and the entailment label is explicitly known: as such, this provides a ripe setting for interventional studies on the NLI models' representations, allowing for stronger causal conjectures and a deeper critical analysis of interventional probing methods. In this work, we carry out new and existing representation-level interventions to investigate the effect of these semantic features on NLI classification: we perform amnesic probing (which removes features as directed by learned linear probes) and introduce the mnestic probing variation (which forgets all dimensions except the probe-selected ones). Furthermore, we delve into the limitations of these methods and outline some pitfalls have been obscuring the effectivity of interventional probing studies.

papers.title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in Large Language Model Representations of True/False Datasets
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs compute and linearly represent the truth of factual statements in their internal activations, and introduces mass-mean probing as a simple method that identifies directions more causally implicated in model outputs.
papers.conclusion: The work finds evidence that LLMs linearly represent truth at scale, localizes these representations to specific hidden states, and shows that mass-mean probing is an effective method for identifying causally implicated truth directions.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations of truth emerge with model scale, with larger models developing a more abstract notion of truth applicable across diverse inputs.
Truth representations are localized to a small group of hidden states (over the end-of-sentence punctuation token) in the residual stream.
Simple difference-in-mean (mass-mean) probes generalize as well as other probing techniques (logistic regression, CCS) for larger models and identify directions that are more causally effective in intervention experiments.
Training probes on datasets that include statements and their logical opposites (e.g., cities and neg cities) improves generalization, mitigating the effect of non-truth correlated features.
Probes trained solely on text likelihood (the likely dataset) perform poorly on datasets where truth and probability are anti-correlated, indicating the represented feature is not merely text probability.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on simple, uncontroversial factual statements, so cannot disambiguate truth from closely related features like 'commonly believed' or 'verifiable'.
Studies only models in the LLaMA-2 family, so results may not generalize to all LLMs.
future_direction: Why were interventions with mass-mean probe directions extracted from the likely dataset effective, despite these probes being inaccurate at classification?
Why did mass-mean probing with the cities+neg_cities training data perform poorly for the 70B model, while mass-mean probing with larger_than+smaller_than performed well?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have impressive capabilities, but are prone to outputting falsehoods. Recent work has developed techniques for inferring whether a LLM is telling the truth by training probes on the LLM's internal activations. However, this line of work is controversial, with some authors pointing out failures of these probes to generalize in basic ways, among other conceptual issues. In this work, we use high-quality datasets of simple true/false statements to study in detail the structure of LLM representations of truth, drawing on three lines of evidence: 1. Visualizations of LLM true/false statement representations, which reveal clear linear structure. 2. Transfer experiments in which probes trained on one dataset generalize to different datasets. 3. Causal evidence obtained by surgically intervening in a LLM's forward pass, causing it to treat false statements as true and vice versa. Overall, we present evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements. We also show that simple difference-in-mean probes generalize as well as other probing techniques while identifying directions which are more causally implicated in model outputs.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Emotion Inference in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do autoregressive large language models internally represent and process emotional information to infer emotions from text?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that emotion representations in LLMs are functionally localized to mid-layers and that causal interventions on appraisal concepts can steer emotion inference in psychologically plausible ways.
papers.conclusion: This work provides a mechanistic understanding of emotion inference in LLMs and demonstrates causal intervention methods to control emotion inference, with potential applications in safety and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Emotion representations are functionally localized to specific mid-layers across diverse model families and sizes.
Activation patching reveals that MHSA and FFN units in mid-layers are critical for emotion inference.
Attention patterns in mid-layers shift to emotionally loaded tokens.
Appraisal concepts are linearly represented in the model and their modulation can steer emotion inference.
The structure of emotion representations aligns with cognitive appraisal theory from psychology.
papers.limitation: Focusing only on correctly classified examples may introduce bias toward unambiguous emotional content.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show promising capabilities in predicting human emotions from text. However, the mechanisms through which these models process emotional stimuli remain largely unexplored. Our study addresses this gap by investigating how autoregressive LLMs infer emotions, showing that emotion representations are functionally localized to specific regions in the model. Our evaluation includes diverse model families and sizes and is supported by robustness checks. We then show that the identified representations are psychologically plausible by drawing on cognitive appraisal theory, a well-established psychological framework positing that emotions emerge from evaluations (appraisals) of environmental stimuli. By causally intervening on construed appraisal concepts, we steer the generation and show that the outputs align with theoretical and intuitive expectations. This work highlights a novel way to causally intervene and precisely shape emotional text generation, potentially benefiting safety and alignment in sensitive affective domains.

papers.title: Probing Internal Representations of Multi-Word Verbs in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do transformer-based large language models capture lexical and syntactic properties of multi-word verbs at different neural network layers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that BERT's middle layers best encode distinctions between phrasal and prepositional verbs, and that these representations are likely non-linearly separable, as indicated by high probing accuracy but weak linear separability measured by GDV.
papers.conclusion: The study supports usage-based linguistic claims and shows that neural network representations of multi-word verbs are complex and non-linearly separable, emphasizing the need for comprehensive analytical methods.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers (layers 6-9 for token-based, layers 5-7 for sentence-based) of BERT achieve the highest classification accuracies for distinguishing phrasal and prepositional verbs.
Generalized Discrimination Value (GDV) shows weak linear separability between the two verb types across layers, with best separability in layers 3-4 for token embeddings.
No statistically significant correlation between probing classifier accuracies and GDV values, suggesting that linguistic distinctions may be encoded non-linearly.
Probing classifiers can achieve high accuracy even when linear separability is weak, indicating that non-linear transformations are involved in the representations.
The disconnect between probing accuracy and model's internal processing highlights limitations of probing methods.
papers.limitation:
Probing classifiers may not indicate whether the model actively uses the linguistic properties for processing, as they only detect correlations in embeddings.
GDV only measures linear separability and may not capture non-linearly structured representations.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the internal representations of verb-particle combinations, called multi-word verbs, within transformer-based large language models (LLMs), specifically examining how these models capture lexical and syntactic properties at different neural network layers. Using the BERT architecture, we analyze the representations of its layers for two different verb-particle constructions: phrasal verbs like 'give up' and prepositional verbs like 'look at'. Our methodology includes training probing classifiers on the internal representations to classify these categories at both word and sentence levels. The results indicate that the model's middle layers achieve the highest classification accuracies. To further analyze the nature of these distinctions, we conduct a data separability test using the Generalized Discrimination Value (GDV). While GDV results show weak linear separability between the two verb types, probing classifiers still achieve high accuracy, suggesting that representations of these linguistic categories may be non-linearly separable. This aligns with previous research indicating that linguistic distinctions in neural networks are not always encoded in a linearly separable manner. These findings computationally support usage-based claims on the representation of verb-particle constructions and highlight the complex interaction between neural network architectures and linguistic structures.

papers.title: Intriguing properties of neural networks
papers.research_question: Do individual units in neural networks have semantic meaning, and are neural networks robust to small perturbations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that semantic information in neural networks is contained in the space of activations rather than individual units, and that neural networks are vulnerable to adversarial examples that generalize across models and datasets.
papers.conclusion: Deep neural networks have counter-intuitive properties with respect to unit semantics and discontinuities, and adversarial examples are dense and may affect generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Random directions in the activation space are as semantically interpretable as individual units.
Neural networks are susceptible to adversarial examples—imperceptible perturbations that cause misclassification.
Adversarial examples generalize across models with different hyperparameters.
Adversarial examples generalize across models trained on disjoint datasets.
The instability of networks can be analyzed via Lipschitz bounds of layers, which can be large even in early layers.
papers.limitation:
The set of adversarial negatives is of extremely low probability and thus rarely observed in the test set, but we don't have a deep understanding of how often they appear.
The Lipschitz bounds are upper bounds and do not guarantee the existence of adversarial examples.
future_direction: Compare the effects of adversarial examples for different layers
Investigate how often adversarial negatives appear
Regularize networks by penalizing Lipschitz bounds to improve generalization
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are highly expressive models that have recently achieved state of the art performance on speech and visual recognition tasks. While their expressiveness is the reason they succeed, it also causes them to learn uninterpretable solutions that could have counter-intuitive properties. In this paper we report two such properties. First, we find that there is no distinction between individual high level units and random linear combinations of high level units, according to various methods of unit analysis. It suggests that it is the space, rather than the individual units, that contains of the semantic information in the high layers of neural networks. Second, we find that deep neural networks learn input-output mappings that are fairly discontinuous to a significant extend. We can cause the network to misclassify an image by applying a certain imperceptible perturbation, which is found by maximizing the network's prediction error. In addition, the specific nature of these perturbations is not a random artifact of learning: the same perturbation can cause a different network, that was trained on a different subset of the dataset, to misclassify the same input.

papers.title: Information-Theoretic Probing for Linguistic Structure
papers.research_question: What is the goal of probing for linguistic properties in neural network representations? The paper proposes that probing should be operationalized as estimating mutual information and argues against the common wisdom of using simpler probes.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes an information-theoretic framework for probing that defines probing as estimating mutual information, argues that one should always use the highest-performing probe, and shows theoretically that contextualized embeddings contain no more syntactic information than the original sentence.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that perfect probing can only yield insights about the language itself, not the representations, and suggests future work should focus on formalizing 'ease of extraction'.
papers.key_findings:
Probing should be operationalized as estimating mutual information, and using the best possible probe (even if complex) yields the tightest estimate.
Theoretically, contextualized word embeddings (e.g., BERT) contain exactly the same amount of information about a word-level syntactic task as the original sentence itself.
Empirically, BERT's embeddings provide only a small gain over type-level embeddings (e.g., fastText) for part-of-speech and dependency labeling across 11 languages, with gains often below 12%.
papers.limitation: The gain estimates can be negative due to approximation errors, highlighting the difficulty of approximating the control functions with finite data.
future_direction: Formalizing the notion of 'ease of extraction' of information from representations.
Using probing to understand language rather than the representations themselves.
papers.abstract: The success of neural networks on a diverse set of NLP tasks has led researchers to question how much these networks actually "know" about natural language. Probes are a natural way of assessing this. When probing, a researcher chooses a linguistic task and trains a supervised model to predict annotations in that linguistic task from the network's learned representations. If the probe does well, the researcher may conclude that the representations encode knowledge related to the task. A commonly held belief is that using simpler models as probes is better; the logic is that simpler models will identify linguistic structure, but not learn the task itself. We propose an information-theoretic operationalization of probing as estimating mutual information that contradicts this received wisdom: one should always select the highest performing probe one can, even if it is more complex, since it will result in a tighter estimate, and thus reveal more of the linguistic information inherent in the representation. The experimental portion of our paper focuses on empirically estimating the mutual information between a linguistic property and BERT, comparing these estimates to several baselines. We evaluate on a set of ten typologically diverse languages often underrepresented in NLP research-plus Englishtotalling eleven languages. Our implementation is available in https://github.com/ rycolab/info-theoretic-probing.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Large-Scale Counting in LLMs through a System-2 Strategy
papers.research_question: How can a test-time strategy inspired by System-2 cognitive processes overcome the architectural limitations of LLMs in large-scale counting tasks, and what are the underlying mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a simple test-time strategy that decomposes large counting tasks into smaller sub-problems, enabling LLMs to surpass their architectural limitations and achieve high accuracy, and provides a mechanistic interpretation of how this System-2-like strategy functions within the models.
papers.conclusion: The proposed System-2 test-time strategy effectively overcomes the architectural limitations of LLMs in large-scale counting by decomposing the task, and mechanistic analysis reveals how count information is stored, transferred, and aggregated within the model.
papers.key_findings:
A System-2 strategy combining structured input (partitioning with a separator) and intermediate reasoning steps (Chain-of-Thought) enables LLMs to accurately count large numbers of items, overcoming the performance degradation seen in standard (System-1) counting.
Attention analysis shows that during intermediate reasoning, the model attends strongly to the final item/separator of each partition in middle-to-late layers (e.g., layers 19-23), and during final answer generation, it attends to the intermediate count tokens.
Causal mediation analysis (activation patching) identifies that count information is stored in the final item representations of each partition, transferred via specific attention heads, and aggregated to produce the final total.
The model's internal counting mechanism (System-1) is capacity-limited and degrades for counts beyond approximately 30 items due to transformer depth constraints, explaining the failure on large-scale counting.
Neither structured input alone nor Chain-of-Thought reasoning alone is sufficient for accurate large-scale counting; their combination is necessary.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on a narrow counting task with limited object diversity, using simple repeated nouns in synthetic contexts.
The approach depends on structured prompts and assumes prior knowledge of the model's reliable counting range, which may limit generalization.
The effects of tokenization and number representation are not isolated and may independently influence the results.
future_direction: Explore further applications of this strategy to complex reasoning tasks in language and beyond.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs), despite strong performance on complex mathematical problems, exhibit systematic limitations in counting tasks. This issue arises from architectural limits of transformers, where counting is performed across layers, leading to degraded precision for larger counting problems due to depth constraints. To address this limitation, we propose a simple test-time strategy inspired by System-2 cognitive processes that decomposes large counting tasks into smaller, independent sub-problems that the model can reliably solve. We evaluate this approach using observational and causal mediation analyses to understand the underlying mechanism of this System-2-like strategy. Our mechanistic analysis identifies key components: latent counts are computed and stored in the final item representations of each part, transferred to intermediate steps via dedicated attention heads, and aggregated in the final stage to produce the total count. Experimental results demonstrate that this strategy enables LLMs to surpass architectural limitations and achieve high accuracy on large-scale counting tasks. This work provides mechanistic insight into System-2 counting in LLMs and presents a generalizable approach for improving and understanding their reasoning behavior.

papers.title: Interpreting the Latent Structure of Operator Precedence in Language Models
papers.research_question: Does the LLaMA 3.2-3B model encode operator precedence in its internal representations, and how does it perform intermediate computations for arithmetic expressions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that intermediate arithmetic computations are linearly encoded in the residual stream of LLaMA 3.2-3B, particularly after MLP blocks, and that operator precedence is encoded in specific embedding dimensions, which can be altered via partial embedding swap.
papers.conclusion: The model internally performs intermediate computations and encodes operator precedence in its representations, with specific dimensions identifiable and modifiable through interpretability techniques.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate calculations appear in the residual stream and are detectable via logit lens, with peak detection in layers 18-19.
Linear probes show that intermediate computations are linearly encoded in activations after layer 0.
Attention ablation in early layers significantly impairs accuracy and reduces intermediate computation detection.
Operator precedence is linearly encoded in embeddings after the attention layer, as shown by high probe accuracy.
Partial embedding swap can modify model predictions by swapping high-impact dimensions between operators.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive reasoning capabilities but continue to struggle with arithmetic tasks. Prior works largely focus on outputs or prompting strategies, leaving the open question of the internal structure through which models do arithmetic computation. In this work, we investigate whether LLMs encode operator precedence in their internal representations via the open-source instruction-tuned LLaMA 3.2-3B model. We constructed a dataset of arithmetic expressions with three operands and two operators, varying the order and placement of parentheses. Using this dataset, we trace whether intermediate results appear in the residual stream of the instruction-tuned LLaMA 3.2-3B model. We apply interpretability techniques such as logit lens, linear classification probes, and UMAP geometric visualization. Our results show that intermediate computations are present in the residual stream, particularly after MLP blocks. We also find that the model linearly encodes precedence in each operator's embeddings post attention layer. We introduce partial embedding swap, a technique that modifies operator precedence by exchanging high-impact embedding dimensions between operators.

papers.title: Shadow of the (Hierarchical) Tree: Reconciling Symbolic and Predictive Components of the Neural Code for Syntax
papers.research_question: How can symbolic representations and connectionist neural networks be integrated to account for both hierarchical (vertical) and linear/predictive (horizontal) aspects of natural language syntax?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a hybrid neurosymbolic model that reconciles symbolic hierarchical syntax and connectionist linear/predictive processes via oscillatory phase codes, specifically extending the ROSE architecture.
papers.conclusion: A hybrid neurosymbolic approach, using oscillatory phase codes, can reconcile symbolic and predictive components of syntax, providing a path forward for cognitive neuroscience and language modeling.
papers.key_findings:
The ROSE architecture provides a symbolic account of hierarchical syntax via oscillatory mechanisms like phase-amplitude coupling.
Horizontal syntactic information (linear, statistical) can be integrated via predictive coding and statistical inference at lower levels of ROSE.
Oscillatory phase codes (e.g., traveling waves modulating high-frequency spiking) provide a feasible interface between symbolic and statistical representations.
Large language models (LLMs) are more competent at modeling horizontal syntactic information than vertical hierarchical syntax, indicating a limitation in their compositional reasoning.
A mathematical model demonstrates how frontotemporal traveling waves can dynamically modulate high-frequency spiking activity to integrate symbolic and statistical information for morphosyntax.
future_direction: Integrating associationist and predictive neural mechanisms into the existing ROSE architecture.
Mathematical formalization of the ROSE architecture and its hybrid extensions.
Testing the proposed hybrid neurosymbolic model with empirical neural data.
papers.abstract: Natural language syntax can serve as a major test for how to integrate two infamously distinct frameworks: symbolic representations and connectionist neural networks. Building on a recent neurocomputational architecture for syntax (ROSE), I discuss the prospects of reconciling the neural code for hierarchical 'vertical' syntax with linear and predictive 'horizontal' processes via a hybrid neurosymbolic model. I argue that the former can be accounted for via the higher levels of ROSE in terms of vertical phrase structure representations, while the latter can explain horizontal forms of linguistic information via the tuning of the lower levels to statistical and perceptual inferences. One prediction of this is that artificial language models will contribute to the cognitive neuroscience of horizontal morphosyntax, but much less so to hierarchically compositional structures. I claim that this perspective helps resolve many current tensions in the literature. Options for integrating these two neural codes are discussed, with particular emphasis on how predictive coding mechanisms can serve as interfaces between symbolic oscillatory phase codes and population codes for the statistics of linearized aspects of syntax. Lastly, I provide a neurosymbolic mathematical model for how to inject symbolic representations into a neural regime encoding lexico-semantic statistical features.

papers.title: Investigating task-specific prompts and sparse autoencoders for activation monitoring
papers.research_question: How do prompted probing and SAE-based probing compare for activation monitoring in language models, and under what constraints (e.g., data availability, compute) are they most effective?
papers.core_contribution: Prompted probing is a data-efficient and effective method for activation monitoring, especially in low-data regimes. SAE-based probing can be effective when inference-time compute is limited, but prompted probing is recommended when inference-time compute is available.
papers.conclusion: The paper recommends prompted probing when inference-time compute is available due to its data efficiency and generalization. If inference-time compute is limited, SAE-based probing is a good alternative. Straightforward activation probing is reasonable when both inference-time and train-time compute are limited.
papers.key_findings:
Prompted last token probing is the most data-efficient technique and performs well in low-data regimes.
Prompting is important: prompted last token probe outperforms naive last token probe, especially in low-data regimes.
In high-data regimes, all probing techniques (prompted probing, SAE probing, raw last token probing) can outperform zero-shot model output.
SAE max-pooled probing generalizes poorly out-of-distribution compared to prompted probing in some cases.
For sentiment classification, last token probes perform best, and max-pooling across tokens degrades performance.
papers.limitation:
The work does not compare the methods to fine-tuning the model, which is often the method of choice when labeled training data is available.
Estimates of zero-shot monitoring performance are likely pessimistic due to lack of prompt engineering and not using reasoning models or chain-of-thought.
Few-shot prompting did not improve performance in the studied settings, possibly due to context length limitations or the model's inability to extract useful signal.
future_direction: Exploring unsupervised approaches like LAT Scans for monitoring when labeled data is unavailable.
Investigating the mechanisms underlying prompted probing and whether prompted and un-prompted probing rely on shared representations.
More research into model organisms of emergent deceptive monitors to understand collusion risks.
papers.abstract: Language models can behave in unexpected and unsafe ways, and so it is valuable to monitor their outputs. Internal activations of language models encode additional information that could be useful for this. The baseline approach for activation monitoring is some variation of linear probing on a particular layer: starting from a labeled dataset, train a logistic regression classifier on that layer's activations. Recent work has proposed several approaches which may improve on naive linear probing, by leveraging additional computation. One class of techniques, which we call "prompted probing," leverages test time computation to improve monitoring by (1) prompting the model with a description of the monitoring task, and (2) applying a learned linear probe to resulting activations. Another class of techniques uses computation at train time: training sparse autoencoders offline to identify an interpretable basis for the activations, and e.g. max-pooling activations across tokens using that basis before applying a linear probe. However, one can also prompt the model with a description of the monitoring task and use its output directly. We develop and test novel refinements of these methods and compare them against each other. We find asking the model zero-shot is a reasonable baseline when inference-time compute is not limited; however, activation probing methods can substantially outperform this baseline given sufficient training data. Specifically, we recommend prompted probing when inference-time compute is available, due to its superior data efficiency and good generalization performance. Alternatively, if inference-time compute is limited, we find SAE-based probing methods outperform raw activation probing.

papers.title: Grad-CAM: Visual Explanations from Deep Networks via Gradient-Based Localization
papers.research_question: How can we produce visual explanations for decisions from a large class of CNN-based models to make them more transparent and explainable?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Grad-CAM, a technique that uses gradients flowing into the final convolutional layer to produce coarse localization maps highlighting important image regions for a prediction, applicable to a wide variety of CNN model families without architectural changes or re-training.
papers.conclusion: Grad-CAM is an effective visualization technique for understanding CNN decisions, providing insights into model behavior, failure modes, and biases, and has been successfully applied to image classification, captioning, and VQA tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Grad-CAM produces class-discriminative localization maps that generalize the earlier CAM approach to a broader range of CNN architectures.
Grad-CAM visualizations help diagnose model failure modes, showing that seemingly unreasonable predictions have reasonable explanations.
Grad-CAM is robust to adversarial perturbations and can identify dataset biases, aiding in model generalization and fairness.
Human studies show that Grad-CAM explanations help users establish appropriate trust in predictions and discern a stronger network from a weaker one.
Grad-CAM can be combined with fine-grained visualizations (Guided Backpropagation) to create Guided Grad-CAM, which is both high-resolution and class-discriminative.
papers.limitation:
Grad-CAM produces coarse, low-resolution heatmaps (e.g., 14x14 for VGG/AlexNet).
The discriminative ability of Grad-CAM reduces when applied to earlier convolutional layers or at downsampling layers in architectures like ResNet.

papers.title: StressPrompt: Does Stress Impact Large Language Models and Human Performance Similarly?
papers.research_question: Does stress impact Large Language Models and human performance similarly? This study explores whether LLMs exhibit stress responses similar to humans and whether their performance fluctuates under different stress-inducing prompts.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the StressPrompt dataset and stress scanner to evaluate LLMs under stress, finding that LLMs exhibit human-like stress-performance patterns, with optimal performance under moderate stress.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit performance patterns similar to humans under stress, with moderate stress enhancing capabilities like reasoning and instruction following, while excessive stress impairs tasks like bias detection, suggesting that LLMs have captured human-like stress-performance dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs perform optimally under moderate stress and decline under low and high stress, consistent with the Yerkes-Dodson law.
Stress prompts significantly alter the internal states of LLMs, changing neural representations as measured by PCA on hidden states.
Different LLMs show varying sensitivity to stress, with architecture and training influencing responses.
Task complexity affects optimal stress levels, with complex tasks performing better at lower stress.
Stress impacts emotional intelligence and bias detection differently, improving emotional intelligence under moderate stress but worsening bias detection under high stress.
papers.abstract: Human beings often experience stress, which can significantly influence their performance. This study explores whether Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit stress responses similar to those of humans and whether their performance fluctuates under different stress-inducing prompts. To investigate this, we developed a novel set of prompts, termed StressPrompt, designed to induce varying levels of stress. These prompts were derived from established psychological frameworks and carefully calibrated based on ratings from human participants. We then applied these prompts to several LLMs to assess their responses across a range of tasks, including instruction-following, complex reasoning, and emotional intelligence. The findings suggest that LLMs, like humans, perform optimally under moderate stress, consistent with the Yerkes-Dodson law. Notably, their performance declines under both low and high-stress conditions. Our analysis further revealed that these StressPrompts significantly alter the internal states of LLMs, leading to changes in their neural representations that mirror human responses to stress. This research provides critical insights into the operational robustness and flexibility of LLMs, demonstrating the importance of designing AI systems capable of maintaining high performance in real-world scenarios where stress is prevalent, such as in customer service, healthcare, and emergency response contexts. Moreover, this study contributes to the broader AI research community by offering a new perspective on how LLMs handle different scenarios and their similarities to human cognition.

papers.title: Brittle Minds, Fixable Activations: Understanding Belief Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do internal belief representations emerge in language models? Are they structured or spurious? How robust are they to prompt variations? Can they be strengthened?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that belief representations in language models improve with model size and fine-tuning, are structured yet brittle to prompt variations, and can be strengthened using contrastive activation addition to correct wrong Theory of Mind inferences.
papers.conclusion: Belief representations in language models are structured but brittle, and they can be strengthened via activation editing, offering a path toward more reliable Theory of Mind reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Belief representations emerge in consistent patterns across models, improve with model size, and benefit significantly from fine-tuning, especially in smaller models.
Control tasks and PCA show that belief representations are structured and not spurious.
Representations of others' beliefs are brittle to semantically neutral prompt variations.
Contrastive activation addition (CAA) can strengthen belief representations and improve ToM performance across different tasks.
CAA steering vectors are general and transferable to other ToM tasks, yielding substantial performance gains.
papers.limitation:
The study focused on one dataset (BigToM) and a limited set of model families due to computational constraints.
The approach could be extended to other mental states beyond beliefs.
future_direction: Exploring how different types of fine-tuning influence the emergence of internal belief representations.
Developing robustness benchmarks and new approaches to improve generalization of belief representations.
Directly embedding perspective-taking circuits into model architectures.
papers.abstract: Despite growing interest in Theory of Mind (ToM) tasks for evaluating language models (LMs), little is known about how LMs internally represent mental states of self and others. Understanding these internal mechanisms is critical - not only to move beyond surface-level performance, but also for model alignment and safety, where subtle misattributions of mental states may go undetected in generated outputs. In this work, we present the first systematic investigation of belief representations in LMs by probing models across different scales, training regimens, and prompts - using control tasks to rule out confounds. Our experiments provide evidence that both model size and fine-tuning substantially improve LMs' internal representations of others' beliefs, which are structured - not mere by-products of spurious correlations - yet brittle to prompt variations. Crucially, we show that these representations can be strengthened: targeted edits to model activations can correct wrong ToM inferences.

papers.title: When Can Transformers Count to n?
papers.research_question: What are the fundamental limitations of transformers on basic counting tasks, and how does the difficulty scale with embedding dimension, context length, and vocabulary size?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals a sharp theoretical phase transition in transformers' ability to count, governed by the relationship between embedding dimension and vocabulary size. When the vocabulary exceeds the embedding dimension, counting becomes numerically unstable and practically unlearnable.
papers.conclusion: Transformers have a fundamental geometric bottleneck for counting tasks when vocabulary size exceeds embedding dimension, suggesting that relying on standard parallel attention is insufficient and external tools or sequential memory systems may be necessary.
papers.key_findings:
When the embedding dimension is at least as large as the vocabulary size, transformers can perfectly maintain token counts using orthogonal embeddings.
When the vocabulary size exceeds the embedding dimension, interference between non-orthogonal token representations forces network weights to scale polynomially, rendering exact counting numerically unstable and unlearnable.
Empirical training of small transformers shows a strict performance drop at the theoretical d=m threshold and catastrophic out-of-distribution failure when scaling vocabulary or context length.
State-of-the-art pretrained language models (Gemini, Gemma, Llama, Qwen, Phi) suffer from similar vulnerabilities, with performance degrading as vocabulary size or sequence length increases.
The vocabulary size, not just context length, fundamentally dictates the difficulty of aggregation tasks like counting in transformers.
papers.limitation: The theoretical framework's reliance on bounded Lipschitz constants to evaluate deep transformers; extending communication complexity lower bounds to deeper models without strict Lipschitz assumptions remains an open challenge.
future_direction: Exploring how the fundamental bottleneck behaves in massive-scale frontier models (100B+ parameters).
Rethinking standard discrete tokenization to improve algorithmic generalization, e.g., via continuous or random embeddings.
Using mechanistic interpretability to analyze the exact suboptimal heuristics transformers converge to during the d < m regime.
papers.abstract: Large language models based on the transformer architectures can solve highly complex tasks. But are there simple tasks that such models cannot solve? Here we focus on very simple counting tasks, that involve counting how many times a token in the vocabulary have appeared in a string. We show that if the dimension of the transformer state is linear in the context length, this task can be solved. However, the solution we propose does not scale beyond this limit, and we provide theoretical arguments for why it is likely impossible for a size limited transformer to implement this task. Our empirical results demonstrate the same phase-transition in performance, as anticipated by the theoretical argument. Our results demonstrate the importance of understanding how transformers can solve simple tasks.

papers.title: Do I Know This Entity? Knowledge Awareness and Hallucinations in Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the mechanisms behind hallucinations in language models, specifically regarding entity recognition and knowledge awareness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers entity recognition directions in the representation space that encode knowledge awareness and shows they causally affect knowledge refusal and hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that language models have internal representations of knowledge awareness that affect refusal and hallucinations, and that chat fine-tuning repurposes this existing mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders uncover directions in the representation space that detect whether the model recognizes an entity as known or unknown.
These entity recognition directions generalize across diverse entity types (players, movies, cities, songs).
The directions causally affect knowledge refusal: steering can induce the model to refuse on known entities or hallucinate on unknown entities.
The directions disrupt the attention of downstream heads in the factual recall circuit, suppressing attribute extraction.
Early entity recognition directions regulate the model's expression of knowledge uncertainty, and uncertainty directions are predictive of incorrect answers.
papers.limitation: The methodology for labeling entities as known or unknown might introduce inaccuracies, as the model could guess attributes or fail to recall specific attributes while knowing about the entity.
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in large language models are a widespread problem, yet the mechanisms behind whether models will hallucinate are poorly understood, limiting our ability to solve this problem. Using sparse autoencoders as an interpretability tool, we discover that a key part of these mechanisms is entity recognition, where the model detects if an entity is one it can recall facts about. Sparse autoencoders uncover meaningful directions in the representation space, these detect whether the model recognizes an entity, e.g. detecting it doesn't know about an athlete or a movie. This suggests that models can have self-knowledge: internal representations about their own capabilities. These directions are causally relevant: capable of steering the model to refuse to answer questions about known entities, or to hallucinate attributes of unknown entities when it would otherwise refuse. We demonstrate that despite the sparse autoencoders being trained on the base model, these directions have a causal effect on the chat model's refusal behavior, suggesting that chat finetuning has repurposed this existing mechanism. Furthermore, we provide an initial exploration into the mechanistic role of these directions in the model, finding that they disrupt the attention of downstream heads that typically move entity attributes to the final token.

papers.title: Vector Symbolic Architectures answer Jackendoff's challenges for cognitive neuroscience
papers.research_question: Can Vector Symbolic Architectures meet Jackendoff's four challenges for cognitive neuroscience?
papers.core_contribution: Vector Symbolic Architectures can meet Jackendoff's four challenges for cognitive neuroscience, providing a connectionist basis for symbolic processing.
papers.conclusion: Vector Symbolic Architectures meet Jackendoff's challenges due to their algebraic properties and straightforward physical implementations, but they are relatively unknown because they depend on good design rather than training.
papers.key_findings:
VSAs address the binding problem by using elementwise multiplication for binding, allowing fast construction of novel composite structures.
VSAs handle multiple instances of the same token through superposition and binding with distinct attributes, using frame-like representations.
VSAs implement variables and substitutions through binding operations, enabling productive language rules.
VSAs represent working memory and long-term memory with the same vector dimensionality, making the boundary between them transparent.
VSAs are suitable for cognitive modelling but require good design rather than automated training, making them difficult to work with at higher architectural levels.
papers.limitation:
There is no currently available representational architecture and cognitive architecture that implements fully variable, input driven composition.
VSAs are very difficult to work with at the level of complete representational architectures and cognitive architectures, requiring good design rather than automated training.
future_direction: Developing enhanced recurrent associative memories that can recognize novel composites by retrieving components and generating mappings.
Extending VSA analysis to the representational and cognitive architecture levels.
papers.abstract: Jackendoff (2002) posed four challenges that linguistic combinatoriality and rules of language present to theories of brain function. The essence of these problems is the question of how to neurally instantiate the rapid construction and transformation of the compositional structures that are typically taken to be the domain of symbolic processing. He contended that typical connectionist approaches fail to meet these challenges and that the dialogue between linguistic theory and cognitive neuroscience will be relatively unproductive until the importance of these problems is widely recognised and the challenges answered by some technical innovation in connectionist modelling. This paper claims that a little-known family of connectionist models (Vector Symbolic Architectures) are able to meet Jackendoff's challenges.

papers.title: No Answer Needed: Predicting LLM Answer Accuracy from Question-Only Linear Probes
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) anticipate when they will answer correctly?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that a simple linear probe on residual stream activations can predict an LLM's forthcoming answer correctness, revealing a linearly separable 'factual correctness' signal that generalizes across knowledge domains but fails for mathematical reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The analysis advances understanding of how LLMs encode self-assessment, providing evidence for a general 'Factual Correctness' direction while highlighting the structural distinctness of reasoning capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
A correctness signal is linearly separable in the activation space and generalizes from trivia questions to other factual knowledge datasets.
The correctness direction fails to generalize to mathematical reasoning tasks (GSM8K), indicating a structural misalignment between factual and arithmetic correctness.
Linear separability of correctness is low in early layers and saturates at intermediate transformer layers.
For models that answer 'I don't know', doing so strongly correlates with the probe score, suggesting the same direction captures implicit confidence.
The in-advance correctness signal is strongest and most consistent for the largest model tested (Llama 3.3 70B).
papers.limitation: The learned correctness direction does not generalize to arithmetic-reasoning tasks (GSM8K).
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) anticipate when they will answer correctly? To study this, we extract activations after a question is read but before any tokens are generated, and train linear probes to predict whether the model's forthcoming answer will be correct. Across three open-source model families ranging from 7 to 70 billion parameters, projections on this "in-advance correctness direction" trained on generic trivia questions predict success in distribution and on diverse out-of-distribution knowledge datasets, indicating a deeper signal than dataset-specific spurious features, and outperforming black-box baselines and verbalised predicted confidence. Predictive power saturates in intermediate layers and, notably, generalisation falters on questions requiring mathematical reasoning. Moreover, for models responding "I don't know", doing so strongly correlates with the probe score, indicating that the same direction also captures confidence. By complementing previous results on truthfulness and other behaviours obtained with probes and sparse auto-encoders, our work contributes essential findings to elucidate LLM internals.

papers.title: What do language models model? Transformers, automata, and the format of thought
papers.research_question: What do large language models actually model? Do they tell us something about human capacities, or are they models of the corpus we’ve trained them on?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that transformers model the corpus rather than human linguistic capacities, due to the linear format of the residual stream, and they do so by emulating shortcut automata as suggested by Liu et al. (2022).
papers.conclusion: Language models are not modeling human thought but have learned to use language as a technology in a different way, by emulating automata that generate the corpus via shortcut solutions.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers exhibit permutation invariance (unmasked) or substring invariance (masked), which implies the residual stream has at most a linear format.
Human cognitive science indicates that linguistic capabilities require supralinear formats for computation.
Therefore, transformers do not process language in the way humans do and do not model human linguistic capacities.
Transformers can be understood as calculating the input-to-state function of an automaton that generates the corpus, using parallel 'shortcut' solutions.
The transformer architecture is powerful because it eschews structured representations in favor of learning transformations that capture the structure of the domain.
papers.limitation:
The paper focuses on very simple LLMs: encoder-only transformers performing next-token autoregressive tasks.
The paper is a draft in progress and the author is not entirely happy with it, though the general argument is stood by.
papers.abstract: What do large language models actually model? Do they tell us something about human capacities, or are they models of the corpus we've trained them on? I give a non-deflationary defence of the latter position. Cognitive science tells us that linguistic capabilities in humans rely supralinear formats for computation. The transformer architecture, by contrast, supports at best a linear formats for processing. This argument will rely primarily on certain invariants of the computational architecture of transformers. I then suggest a positive story about what transformers are doing, focusing on Liu et al. (2022)'s intriguing speculations about shortcut automata. I conclude with why I don't think this is a terribly deflationary story. Language is not (just) a means for expressing inner state but also a kind of 'discourse machine' that lets us make new language given appropriate context. We have learned to use this technology in one way; LLMs have also learned to use it too, but via very different means.

papers.title: Language Models Understand Us, Poorly
papers.research_question: What does it mean for language models to understand human language, and do current and future models achieve such understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Argues that internal representations are sufficient for language understanding, critiques the Scaling Paradigm, and advocates for probing model internals to advance the science of understanding.
papers.conclusion: Current language models have limited understanding due to under-specified data, and scaling alone may not suffice without focusing on internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Understanding-as-representation is sufficient for language understanding, while as-reliability is necessary but not sufficient.
Current language models are limited by under-specification of meaning in their training data.
The Scaling Paradigm may be computationally infeasible for achieving human-like understanding.
Probing model internals is essential to advance the science of understanding.
Adding more modalities and human language aspects is needed for better models.
papers.limitation: The paper presents only one perspective and may not fully cover diverse fields or be ultimately correct.
future_direction: Probe model internals
Add more of human language such as intersubjective, multi-agent environments
Measure what models can learn
papers.abstract: Some claim language models understand us. Others won’t hear it. To clarify, I investigate three views of human language understanding: as-mapping, as-reliability and as-representation. I argue that while behavioral reliability is necessary for understanding, internal representations are sufficient; they climb the right hill. I review state-of-the-art language and multi-modal models: they are pragmatically challenged by under-specification of form. I question the Scaling Paradigm: limits on resources may prohibit scaled-up models from approaching understanding. Last, I describe how as-representation advances a science of understanding. We need work which probes model internals, adds more of human language, and measures what models can learn.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Space and Time
papers.research_question: Do large language models learn coherent linear representations of space and time, i.e., do they form a world model?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models learn linear representations of space and time that are robust to prompting and unified across entity types, and individual 'space' and 'time' neurons exist that encode these coordinates.
papers.conclusion: Modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover spatial and temporal coordinates from internal activations, with performance increasing with model size and plateauing in middle layers.
Spatial and temporal features are linearly represented, as nonlinear probes do not improve performance.
Representations are robust to variations in prompting, though random tokens or capitalization degrade performance.
Probes generalize across entity types and to held-out geographic or temporal blocks, indicating unified representations.
Individual neurons exist that are highly predictive of space and time, and causal interventions confirm their importance.
papers.limitation:
Data comes only from English Wikipedia, skewing towards the Anglosphere, and entity type distribution is not uniform.
The true extent and structure of spatial and temporal representations remain unclear.
future_direction: Extracting representations in the model’s coordinate system rather than human coordinates, e.g., with sparse autoencoders.
Studying how these spatiotemporal representations are learned, recalled, and used internally across training checkpoints.
Investigating potential parallels with biological place and grid cells in the brain.
papers.abstract: The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have sparked debate over whether such systems just learn an enormous collection of superficial statistics or a set of more coherent and grounded representations that reflect the real world. We find evidence for the latter by analyzing the learned representations of three spatial datasets (world, US, NYC places) and three temporal datasets (historical figures, artworks, news headlines) in the Llama-2 family of models. We discover that LLMs learn linear representations of space and time across multiple scales. These representations are robust to prompting variations and unified across different entity types (e.g. cities and landmarks). In addition, we identify individual "space neurons" and "time neurons" that reliably encode spatial and temporal coordinates. While further investigation is needed, our results suggest modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.

papers.title: Extending a Mathematical Theory of the Emergence of Knowledge from the Experience to Capture Learning Dynamics in Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers' learning dynamics emerge from the structure of training data, and how does this relate to human semantic development?
papers.core_contribution: Extends a mathematical theory of learning dynamics to minimal transformers, demonstrating that learning trajectories are predictable from data structure and mirror human semantic development.
papers.conclusion: The work provides initial steps toward understanding how transformers learn, demonstrating that experience guides learning in a way that mirrors human semantic development, and the mathematical theory helps capture these dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Learning occurs in two phases: fast reduction of loss-between via relation information, and slower reduction of loss-within via item information through attention.
Learning dynamics follow sigmoidal trajectories for dataset dimensions, as predicted by deep linear network theory.
The model exhibits progressive differentiation of concepts, learning broader categories before finer ones.
The model shows U-shaped learning for certain features, such as overgeneralization of properties.
Embeddings from the minimal transformer correlate with those from larger LLMs, suggesting relevance to scaled-up models.
papers.limitation: The study uses a simplified toy dataset and minimal transformer architecture, which may not fully capture complexities of natural language and larger models.
future_direction: Extending models and training sets to more natural language datasets.
Exploring how attentional strategies emerge for handling longer contextual dependencies.
papers.abstract: The Transformer architecture used in LLMs has garnered widespread attention due to these model's human-like conceptual knowledge and language understanding, yet understanding how these models' capabilities result from experience-guided learning, and connecting this learning process with the structure in their training data, can seem intractable. Here we present preliminary steps to characterizing the developmental trajectory of a minimal Transformer trained on a next-token prediction task, using a simple dataset with quantifiable uncertainty and a simple, intuitively characterizable structure that captures some aspects of natural semantic structure learned by LLMs from large datasets. We show how the dynamic learning process of this model is a predictable consequence of the structure of the training data, exhibiting attested features of human semantic development, as captured in a theory of neural network learning dynamics (Saxe et. al. 2019) previously used to capture such dynamics in a network originally introduced by Rumelhart & Todd (1993).

papers.title: Confidence is Not Competence
papers.research_question: Why do large language models exhibit a disconnect between their internal confidence and actual problem-solving competence?
papers.core_contribution: The confidence-competence gap in LLMs is mechanistically explained by a decoupled two-system architecture: a high-dimensional assessment manifold for belief and a low-dimensional execution manifold for competence, with a sharp transition between them.
papers.conclusion: The confidence-competence gap is due to a decoupled two-system architecture, suggesting future work should focus on controlling the low-dimensional dynamics of execution rather than high-level assessment states.
papers.key_findings:
A linear probe can decode the model's 'solvability belief' from internal states, revealing a geometrically coherent belief axis.
Causal interventions that steer the belief state do not affect task performance, indicating the belief is causally inert.
The assessment manifold has high linear effective dimensionality, while the execution manifold is low-dimensional.
There is a sharp cognitive collapse from the assessment to execution phase, indicating a sequential two-system architecture.
This reveals an 'Assessment Brain' and an 'Execution Brain' that are geometrically and functionally distinct.
papers.limitation:
The findings are limited to tasks with unambiguous ground-truth solutions (e.g., math, logic, coding) and may not generalize to open-ended creative tasks.
The scaling laws of the cognitive collapse phenomenon are unknown and may vary with model size.
future_direction: Generalizing the 'Two Brains' model to open-ended creative tasks.
Studying the scaling laws of the cognitive collapse in larger models.
Developing 'mechanistic audits' to test Assessment and Execution brains separately.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit a puzzling disconnect between their asserted confidence and actual problem-solving competence. We offer a mechanistic account of this decoupling by analyzing the geometry of internal states across two phases - pre-generative assessment and solution execution. A simple linear probe decodes the internal "solvability belief" of a model, revealing a well-ordered belief axis that generalizes across model families and across math, code, planning, and logic tasks. Yet, the geometries diverge - although belief is linearly decodable, the assessment manifold has high linear effective dimensionality as measured from the principal components, while the subsequent reasoning trace evolves on a much lower-dimensional manifold. This sharp reduction in geometric complexity from thought to action mechanistically explains the confidence-competence gap. Causal interventions that steer representations along the belief axis leave final solutions unchanged, indicating that linear nudges in the complex assessment space do not control the constrained dynamics of execution. We thus uncover a two-system architecture - a geometrically complex assessor feeding a geometrically simple executor. These results challenge the assumption that decodable beliefs are actionable levers, instead arguing for interventions that target the procedural dynamics of execution rather than the high-level geometry of assessment.

papers.title: The Process of Categorical Clipping at the Core of the Genesis of Concepts in Synthetic Neural Cognition
papers.research_question: How does the process of categorical outlining (clipping) manifest in terms of cognitive and categorical properties within neural networks, specifically how does the aggregation function separate a form from a background?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates the process of categorical clipping in neural networks, showing how neurons create new functional categories by selectively extracting subdimensions from precursor categories through a process of reflective abstraction, involving categorical reduction, selectivity, and segmentation of embedding dimensions.
papers.conclusion: Categorical outlining in synthetic cognition is a process of reflective abstraction that constructs new categories by recombining selected embedding dimensions from precursor categories, rather than merely extracting pre-existing forms.
papers.key_findings:
Categorical outlining involves the selective extraction of specific embedding dimensions from the initial embedding space, rather than random selection.
The extracted subdimensions are categorically convergent and homogeneous, indicating a non-random process.
The process is consistent with Piaget's stages of reflective abstraction, involving abstraction, reflection, and reasoning.
Categorical outlining constructs new categories by recombining selected embedding dimensions, rather than simply separating pre-existing forms.
The process demonstrates categorical selectivity, with a minority of tokens becoming 'taken' and associated with specific embedding dimensions.
papers.abstract: This article investigates, within the field of neuropsychology of artificial intelligence, the process of categorical segmentation performed by language models. This process involves, across different neural layers, the creation of new functional categorical dimensions to analyze the input textual data and perform the required tasks. Each neuron in a multilayer perceptron (MLP) network is associated with a specific category, generated by three factors carried by the neural aggregation function: categorical priming, categorical attention, and categorical phasing. At each new layer, these factors govern the formation of new categories derived from the categories of precursor neurons. Through a process of categorical clipping, these new categories are created by selectively extracting specific subdimensions from the preceding categories, constructing a distinction between a form and a categorical background. We explore several cognitive characteristics of this synthetic clipping in an exploratory manner: categorical reduction, categorical selectivity, separation of initial embedding dimensions, and segmentation of categorical zones.

papers.title: A matter of framing: The impact of linguistic formalism on probing results
papers.research_question: Does the choice of linguistic formalism affect probing results in role semantics?
papers.core_contribution: The choice of linguistic formalism has a linguistically meaningful impact on probing results, and layer probing can detect subtle differences between implementations of the same formalism.
papers.conclusion: Linguistic formalism is an important factor to be accounted for in probing studies, and future work should consider cross-formalism comparisons.
papers.key_findings:
Layer utilization for role labeling differs between predicate and argument tokens.
The formalism affects layer utilization: PropBank predicate encoding relies on syntactic layers, while VerbNet and FrameNet rely on lexical layers.
Anchor task analysis shows that role probes for different formalisms align with different lower-level tasks.
Layer probing can detect subtle differences between implementations of the same formalism in different languages.
Semantic proto-role properties, especially Proto-Agent ones, can be extracted from pre-trained BERT.
